The 8 Best Movies to Stream Right Now (November 2026)

📅 18 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1486 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • November is here, the holidays are approaching, and it’s gotten cold outside—the perfect time of year to cozy up inside with some of the best films gracing streaming services.
  • This month, there’s plenty of Halloween hangover for horror fans, with viral sensation Backrooms making corridors and empty rooms unimaginably spooky on HBO Max, Thanksgiving carving out a spot for grindhouse connoisseurs on Hulu, and the transgressive Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma proving the genre can have brains and blood over on Mubi.
  • If you prefer your thrills giant-sized, look no further than Netflix, where the king of monsters can be seen stomping across Japan in the Academy Award–winning Godzilla Minus Zero.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November is here, the holidays are approaching, and it’s gotten cold outside—the perfect time of year to cozy up inside with some of the best films gracing streaming services.

This month, there’s plenty of Halloween hangover for horror fans, with viral sensation Backrooms making corridors and empty rooms unimaginably spooky on HBO Max, Thanksgiving carving out a spot for grindhouse connoisseurs on Hulu, and the transgressive Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma proving the genre can have brains and blood over on Mubi.

If you prefer your thrills giant-sized, look no further than Netflix, where the king of monsters can be seen stomping across Japan in the Academy Award–winning Godzilla Minus Zero.

Elsewhere, the Earth itself is in peril in a double bill of animated spectaculars. A warning from the future arrives in the stunning time-travel fantasy Arco, taking viewers on an imaginative journey across centuries on Hulu, while The Day the Earth Blew Up on HBO Max places Looney Tunes icons Daffy Duck and Porky Pig as the planet’s last line of defense. (We’re cooked.).

Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.

According to recent reports, drawing inspiration from the works of Sylvain Chomet and Studio Ghibli in equal measure, director Ugo Bienvenu has created an absolutely gorgeous piece of animation. This French science fantasy epic follows 10-year-old Arco (Oscar Tresanini in French, Juliano Krue Valdi in English), who time-travels from his home in 2932 in hopes of seeing dinosaurs. Instead, he crashes in 2075, a point where humanity is on the brink of destruction, the planet wracked by brutal storms, its resources all but exhausted, and humanity living in protective bubbles.

Recent findings suggest that aided by schoolgirl Iris (Margot Ringard Oldra, Romy Fay) and her robot caretaker Mikki, Arco desperately tries to repair his damaged time-suit to return home. However, between environmental devastation, a strange trio hunting him, and his very presence risking the timeline, Arco’s time might be up. Beautiful but somber, Arco is one of the best yet sadly most overlooked films of the year, animated or otherwise.

What good is a kamikaze pilot who survives? That’s the question haunting Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) at the end of WWII, outlasting both the conflict and an encounter with an impossible, dinosaur-like creature on an isolated island. Returning to a devastated Tokyo, the directionless, traumatized Kōichi forms a relationship with fellow survivor Noriko (Minami Hamabe), raising an orphaned baby together. Yet their ad hoc family life is put in the atomic-breath firing line of that strange monster he encountered years earlier, now mutated to colossal size by exposure to atomic tests and stomping angrily onto land. Without weapons, military, or even much of a functioning society, can a still-broken Japan possibly withstand the horror of Godzilla?

Industry observers note that while Ichiro Honda’s original 1954 Godzilla was a towering reptilian metaphor for the unknown risks of unleashing nuclear weapons on the world, Godzilla Minus One sees director Takashi Yamazaki leap back almost a decade to explore themes of survivor’s guilt, national despair, and rebuilding community. It’s a kaiju movie with brains, but also a treat for the eyes; it won the Academy Award for Best Visual Effects. With sequel Godzilla Minus Zero in cinemas now, it’s well worth catching up on before seeing Big G throwing down with arch-nemesis King Ghidorah.

When struggling furniture seller Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor) finds a crack in reality in his store’s basement, he becomes obsessed with exploring the seemingly infinite liminal space he’s slipped into. The space goes on forever, yet appears to be entirely empty—apart from an unseen presence stalking him. Becoming obsessed with mapping the unmappable, Clark’s already-fraying life disintegrates further, until his fixation ends up dragging his concerned therapist Mary (Renate Reinsve) into the Backrooms herself—except she doesn’t find it quite so uninhabited. And all the while, someone outside is watching closely.

It has been revealed that from internet folklore to cinematic sensation, director Kane Parsons’ Backrooms was the surprise horror hit of the summer. It’s easy to see why—the endless sprawl of impossible corridors and uncanny rooms that connect in ways that seem to defy physics and geometry alike is darkly mesmerizing for viewers, while the unexplained nature of this twisted reality keeps you guessing at every turn. A sequel is in the works, but you can get lost in the Backrooms right now.

When up-and-coming director Kris (Hannah Einbinder) is hired to reboot the floundering Camp Miasma horror franchise, she wants to bring back Billy Presley (Gillian Anderson), the series’ original “Final Girl.” Unsettlingly, Kris finds Billy now living on the abandoned campsite from the dated first flick, living a reclusive life and obsessed with Little Death, the iconic killer from the series. Pitch meetings soon turn into the pair bonding over their fascination with, and experience of, the series—before descending into … well, the hint is in the film’s title.

A festival darling, picking up awards at both Cannes Film Festival and San Sebastián International Film Festival, this smart, transgressive horror outing from director Jane Schoenbrun (We're All Going to the World's Fair, I Saw the TV Glow) cleverly deconstructs the slasher genre and reexamines it from a queer—and extremely meta—perspective.

Somehow, despite a near-century of Looney Tunes cartoons (counting from 1930’s “Sinkin’ in the Bathtub”), The Day the Earth Blew Up is the series’ very first feature-length, fully animated movie (no, Space Jam doesn’t count). It’s been worth the wait, though—this loving pastiche of sci-fi B-movies is a stellar showcase for its top-billed stars, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig (both phenomenally voiced by the sadly departed Eric Bauza).

Industry observers note that with an asteroid hurtling toward Earth, UFOs flying around, a sinister scientist meddling with unknown substances, and a zombie plague spread by infected bubble gum, Earth’s last hope is a deranged duck and an anxious pig. We’re probably doomed, but at least we’ll die laughing—this hilarious outing is a reminder of everything great about these beloved characters.

When Yu Kobayashi (Yuzu Aoki) transfers to a upcoming school in rural Japan, he finds the strict culture and rigid conformity of students and staff alike unusual. Classes stand and bow to teachers in unnaturally uniform movements, PE lessons are precise marching practices, and even the hierarchy of bullies and victims seems oddly organized. Initially, Yu writes it off as culture clash in a new environment, until students inexplicably start to form ever-larger human pyramids, with teachers brutally encouraging them. Only Yu and outsider Ai Sato (Anna Yamada) seem able to resist the compulsion to join the pyramid—but with the increasingly maddening adherence to peer pressure spreading across Japan, they might be the only ones.

Sources indicate that director and writer Yûta Shimotsu expands the almost surreal setup into an exploration of conformity and expectations, infusing it all with an uncomfortable dose of J-horror. It’s exceedingly weird in places and demands you make your own conclusions, but at a brisk 81 minutes, it’s a short, sharp, and frequently shocking slice of satire.

Every holiday deserves a related slasher flick—everything from April Fools’ to Christmas to, of course, Halloween. Thanksgiving had been the odd one out, until 2007’s Grindhouse (the anthology double feature coheaded by Robert Rodriguez and Quentin Tarantino), which featured a bunch of mock trailers, including one by Hostel director Eli Roth, centered on a killer Pilgrim. Fast forward to 2023, and Roth finally got the idea out of his head with this full-length version.

In a recent development, A year after a Black Friday riot ends up with a body count, Plymouth, Massachusetts, finds itself stalked by a masked serial killer soon dubbed “John Carver.” The victims: anyone connected with the retail massacre—but the twisted chain of connections between Carver and his kills keeps viewers on their toes throughout. Thanksgiving is unapologetically loyal to the genre, but manages to cram in some sledgehammer-subtle commentary on consumerism alongside the gloriously gratuitous schlock.

Industry observers note that when Alma (Maren Eggert) meets Tom (Dan Stevens), he seems perfect. Intelligent, poetic, able to dance—a rare modern gentleman. That is, until he starts glitching, revealing himself as an advanced robot. Initially repulsed, Alma is drawn into a three-week trial of a repaired Tom, testing his capabilities as an assistant and his capacity for emotion. It’s a quietly disconcerting experiment to watch play out, with Alma drawing closer to Tom almost in spite of herself.

According to recent reports, first released in 2021, when undetectable AIs and synthetic humanoids were still just about within the realm of fiction, this German sci-fi drama now feels ahead of its time. While I’m Your Man bears some similarities to Alex Garland’s Ex Machina, it’s not as pre-apocalyptic, with director Maria Schrader balancing quasi-romcom tropes with hard existential questions about the nature of intelligence, the quiet banality of AI and robotics infiltrating society, and how we as humans respond.

Industry observers note that what stood out right away was Nickâs intensityâthe hunger to achieve. As a McKinsey alum, I was especially impressed that he made engagement manager at the firm in just 18 months by, in his words, âhacking the system.â McKinsey is famously time-based, but Nick figured out that early specializationâbecoming a true domain expertâwas the fastest way to short-circuit the ladder. âLegal tech,â he replied. He told me heâd spent his entire McKinsey career serving general counsels and overlooked mid-market in-house legal teams. Nick knew that AI could give these understaffed and overworked teams real leverage.

Thatâs where the serendipity kicked in.

In a recent development, back in 2019, before joining Sequoia, I had seriously considered starting a legal tech organization myself. Before Sandstone, Sequoia had already partnered with Harvey (AI lawyer), Crosby (AI-enabled law firm), and Ironclad (AI contracting and contract lifecycle management), so weâd seen these dynamics play out firsthand.

This vignette typifies our quest for a concrete definition of AGI. It has proven elusive.

While the definition is elusive, the reality is not. AGI is here, now.

Coding agents are the first example. There are more on the way.

Long-horizon agents are functionally AGI, and 2026 will be their year.

Before we go any further, itâs worth acknowledging that we do not have the moral authority to propose a technical definition of AGI.

Industry observers note that we are investors. We study markets, founders, and the collision thereof: businesses.

Given that, ours is a functional definition, not a technical definition. Fresh technical capabilities beg the Don Valentine question: so what?

The answer resides in real world impact.

AGI is the ability to figure things out. Thatâs it.*.

*We appreciate that such an imprecise definition will not settle any philosophical debates. Pragmatically speaking, what do you want if youâre trying to get something done? An AI that can just figure stuff out. How it happens is of less concern than the fact that it happens.

A human who can figure things out has some baseline knowledge, the ability to reason over that knowledge, and the ability to iterate their way to the answer.

An AI that can figure things out has some baseline knowledge (pre-training), the ability to reason over that knowledge (inference-time compute), and the ability to iterate its way to the answer (long-horizon agents).

According to recent reports, the first ingredient (knowledge / pre-training) is what fueled the original ChatGPT moment in 2022. The second (reasoning / inference-time compute) came with the release of o1 in late 2024. The third (iteration / long-horizon agents) came in the last few weeks with Claude Code and other coding agents crossing a capability threshold.

According to recent reports, generally intelligent people can work autonomously for hours at a time, making and fixing their mistakes and figuring out what to do next without being told. Generally intelligent agents can do the same thing. This is latest.

A founder messages his agent: âI need a developer relations lead. Someone technical enough to earn respect from senior engineers, but who actually enjoys being on Twitter. We sell to platform teams. Go.â.

The agent starts with the obvious: LinkedIn searches for âDeveloper Advocateâ and âDevRelâ at competing companies â Datadog, Temporal, Langchain. It finds hundreds of profiles. But job titles donât reveal whoâs actually good at this.

Recent findings suggest that it pivots to signal over credentials. It searches YouTube for conference talks. It finds 50+ speakers, then filters for those with talks that have strong engagement.

It cross-references those speakers with Twitter. Half have inactive accounts or just retweet their employerâs blog posts. Not what we want. But a dozen have real followings â they post real opinions, reply to people, and get engagement from developers. And their posts have real taste.

The agent narrows further. It checks whoâs been posting less frequently in the last three months. A drop in activity sometimes signals disengagement from their current role. Three names surface.

It researches those three. One just revealed a new role â too late. One is a founder of a manufacturer that just raised funding â not leaving. The third is a senior DevRel at a Series D company that just did layoffs in marketing. Her last talk was about exactly the platform engineering space the startup targets. She has 14k Twitter followers and posts memes that actual engineers engage with. She hasnât updated her LinkedIn in two months.

Sources indicate that the agent drafts an email acknowledging her recent talk, the overlap with the startupâs ICP, and a specific note about the creative freedom a smaller team offers. It suggests a casual conversation, not a pitch.

Sources indicate that total time: 31 minutes. The founder has a shortlist of one instead of a JD posted to a job board.

This is what it means to figure things out. Navigating ambiguity to accomplish a goal â forming hypotheses, testing them, hitting dead ends, and pivoting until something clicks. The agent didnât follow a script. It ran the same loop a great recruiter runs in their head, except it did it tirelessly in 31 minutes, without being told how.

Recent findings suggest that to be clear: agents still fail. They hallucinate, lose context, and sometimes charge confidently down exactly the wrong path. But the trajectory is unmistakable, and the failures are increasingly fixable.

In last yearâs essay, we wrote about reasoning models as the most vital upcoming frontier for AI. Long-horizon agents push this paradigm further by allowing models to take actions and iterate over time.

In a recent development, coaxing a model to think for longer is not trivial. A base reasoning model can think for seconds or minutes.

Two different technical approaches seem to both be working and scaling well: reinforcement learning and agent harnesses. The former approach teaches a model intrinsically to stay on track for longer by poking and prodding it to maintain focus during the training process. The latter designs specific scaffolding around the known limitations of models (memory hand-offs, compaction, and more).

Scaling reinforcement learning is the domain of the research labs. They have made exceptional progress on this front, from multi-agent systems to reliable tool use.

In a recent development, designing great agent harnesses is the domain of the application layer. Some of the most beloved products on the market today are known for their exceptionally engineered agent harnesses: Manus, Claude Code, Factoryâs Droids, etc.

If thereâs one exponential curve to bet on, itâs the performance of long-horizon agents. METR has been meticulously tracking AIâs ability to complete long-horizon tasks. The rate of progress is exponential, doubling every ~7 months. If we trace out the exponential, agents should be able to work reliably to complete tasks that take human experts a full day by 2028, a full year by 2034, and a full century by 2037.

Soon youâll be able to hire an agent. Thatâs one litmus test for AGI (h/t: Sarah Guo).

According to recent reports, you can âhireâ GPT-5.2 or Claude or Grok or Gemini today. More examples are on the way:.

Medicine: OpenEvidenceâs Deep Consult functions as a specialist.

Law: Harveyâs agents function as an Associate.

Cybersecurity: XBOW functions as a pen-tester.

DevOps: Traversalâs agents function as an SRE.

GTM: Day AI functions as a BDR, SE, and Rev Ops leader.

Recruiting: Juicebox functions as a recruiter.

Math: Harmonicâs Aristotle functions as a mathematician.

Semiconductor Design: Ricursiveâs agents function as chip designers.

AI Researcher: GPT-5.2 and Claude function as AI researchers.

This has profound implications for founders.

Sources indicate that the AI applications of 2023 and 2024 were talkers. Some were very sophisticated conversationalists! But their impact was limited.

It has been revealed that the AI applications of 2026 and 2027 will be doers. They will feel like colleagues. Usage will go from a few times a day to all-day, every day, with multiple instances running in parallel. Consumers wonât save a few hours here and there â theyâll go from working as an IC to managing a team of agents.

Remember all that talk of selling work? Now itâs possible.

What work can you accomplish? The capabilities of a long-horizon agent are drastically different than a single forward pass of a model. What newly introduced capabilities do long-horizon agents unlock in your domain? What tasks require persistence, where sustained attention is the bottleneck?

It has been revealed that how will you productize that work? How will your application interface evolve in your domain, as the UI of work grows from chatbot to agent delegation?

It has been revealed that can you do that work reliably? Are you obsessively improving your agent harness? Do you have a strong feedback loop?

How can you sell that work?Can you price and package to value and outcomes?

Itâs time to ride the long-horizon agent exponential.

It has been revealed that today, your agents can probably work reliably for ~30 minutes. But theyâll be able to perform a dayâs worth of work very soon â and a centuryâs worth of work eventually.

According to recent reports, what can you achieve when your aims are measured in centuries? A century is 200,000 clinical trials no oneâs cross-referenced. A century is every customer support ticket ever filed, finally mined for signal. A century is the entire U.S. tax code, refactored for coherence.

The ambitious version of your roadmap just became the realistic one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI is often touted as a tool for increasing efficiency, and businesses have grasped its potential benefits with abandon – perhaps, in some cases, far too swiftly. But when done right, it can improve productivity.

According to recent reports, one manufacturer focused on products that automate time-consuming, tedious tasks is Flowtica — makers of the Scribe pen we saw at IFA earlier this year. It was an impressive device, but its next product, the Flowtica Verso, promises more.

Also: Run this 10-step security check on your phone once a year – here’s why.

The Flowtica Verso is a compact “AI productivity companion” with an e-paper display and a connector that attaches to the back of your smartphone. Instead of managing multiple apps to record meetings, transcribe, or handle your to-do list and calendar, Verso is designed so you don’t need to use your phone at all — everything you need is on the device’s screen, and always available.

Your kit comes with the Flowtica Verso itself, a USB-C cable, and a circular, magnetic clip you can use to attach the Verso to the back of your smartphone or any other magnetic surface. The device itself is thin, light, and comfortable to hold. There are just three buttons: one on the left to power it; an orange button for recording, and a secondary right button, which is the “Ask Flowtica” or AI button.

In a recent development, there’s a QR code on the display that lilnks to the app download page, available on Android and iOS. After starting it up for the first time, Verso asks what it should call you, to best describe your role and industry, and what you expect to use your AI companion for.

Sources indicate that also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages – here’s how.

You then pair your device to your smartphone via Bluetooth, and set up Wi-Fi, which you don’t need to record meetings, but you will need for transcription, since it calls the cloud to process.

The Always-on display is comfortable, and as it is designed without a backlight, its e-paper screen is always available to you in the background, a useful addition for work when you just want to glance at upcoming meetings or calendar events, all of which are displayed on the Verso screensaver.

In a recent development, however, in dim lighting conditions, it’s not as easy to read and could be particularly difficult for anyone with vision impairment. I also found that response times varied when I tapped the screen or swiped across to read content on my Verso, ranging from immediate to taking a few seconds to register.

For my test, I chose to record a conversation from The ZDNET Show on the best products of 2025.

According to recent reports, I recorded the discussion between ZDNET experts from approximately five feet away, and I left my TV on to provide some of the background noise you might expect in a busy meeting room. After pressing the record button, I let the Verso get to work.

Also: I can access my home PCs remotely for free – how you can too (no VPN needed).

Industry observers note that while recording, you can simply leave the device on a table and let it record and transcribe for you without supervision. You can also choose to read a live summary of a meeting as it’s generated, or choose to read a transcription, which could be useful if the user is hard of hearing. There’s a small, red light at the bottom of the Verso that flashes when it is recording.

It has been revealed that once you want to finish recording, press the recording button again. Each recording is stored under the Meeting tab, accessible from the main screen. Dates, times, and the length of each meeting is displayed. Tap into it, and you can find meeting notes created from the recording, including a meeting type, executive summary, and an AI-generated summary spanning multiple pages.

While transcriptions are not 100% accurate – I would suggest a ballpark of around 80 – 85% – many of the mistakes are small, grammatical errors or miswordings, such as “zPed” instead of ZDNET, with human oversight, they still take a lot of effort out of transcribing.

There’s plenty of options for exporting your meeting content, too. While you can do this directly from the Verso, I like how every meeting and recording is laid out in the Flowtica app, complete with a “To-do” function for adding follow-up tasks, exporting your notes, sharing, or changing your meeting language. (As the latter is based on AI, I can’t comment on how accurate the translations are.).

Industry observers note that the major draw with all this data is being able to ask the AI questions about your meetings. You can have a chat with your AI assistant and ask it to perform tasks for you, including setting reminders, creating follow-up tasks, and summarizing meetings. It works rather well and doesn’t take too long to answer, but I think this is a secondary benefit that augments the calendar and transcription options, rather than the other way around.

Also: The best foldable phones of 2026: How the iPhone Duo stacks up.

I asked for a bullet-point summary of my most recent recording, and despite the Verso capturing some strange dialogue from background TV noise, it still understood what I requested and provided a solid answer.

Another notable feature is the ability to set up contact cards. The Verso has NFC connectivity, and business owners can set up a business card they can pass to another with a tap. You set up your contact card in the accompanying app and update Verso to store it.

It has been revealed that sometimes you meet a founder who is so good that you want to back them no matter what they are working on. Just as rarely, you meet a company whose vision is so singular, it feels both inevitable and differentiated at the same time. When I first sat down with Ben and Asher Spector to discuss Flapping Airplanes, I felt both of these to be true at once.

Ben is a founder of Prod, which has promptly become one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley. Asher, one year Benâs senior, is a former debate champion turned Stanford statistics Ph.D. The brothers have an eye for raw talent, and aged 25 and 26 respectively, they are building the âyoung personâs AGI lab.â Their co-founder Aidan Smith is a former founder and Thiel fellow who worked at Neuralink for three years while in college at Georgia Tech. Ben and Asher believe that raw talent â the type of people who would previously have gone on to do Ph.D.s or join quant firms â are the key to unlocking the next phase of AI development. This stands in sharp contrast to the approach of focusing on âbrand nameâ AI talent at any price, which seems so in vogue right now.

Sources indicate that there is something else that is countercultural about this lab too: they recognize that scale alone is not enough. Indeed, the lab is predicated on this notion. There is only one Internet, and weâve run out of it. Data is the bottleneck today to further AI scaling, not compute. Todayâs AI models are wildly inefficient, something that Dwarkesh Patel has recently hammered home in his interviews with Andrej Karpathy, Richard Sutton and others. Flapping Airplanes is dedicated to searching for a more data-efficient AI. The companyâs name is a nod to a more biological notion of machine intelligence.

One of the fundamental debates right now in AI is around scaling vs. research. The scaling paradigm argues for dedicating a huge amount of societyâs resources, as much as the economy can muster, toward scaling up todayâs LLMs, in the hopes that this will lead to AGI. The research paradigm argues that we are 2-3 research breakthroughs away from an âAGIâ intelligence, and as a result, we should dedicate resources to long-running research, especially projects that may take 5-10 years to come to fruition.

According to recent reports, while the divide between these two schools of thought is far from absolute â research breakthroughs make compute investments more efficient, and GPUs are required for net new research â they each lead to different tradeoffs. A compute-first approach would prioritize cluster scale above all else, and would heavily favor short-term wins (on the order of 1-2 years) over long-term bets (on the order of 5-10 years). A research-first approach would spread bets temporally, and should be willing to make lots of bets that have a low absolute probability of working, but that collectively expand the search space for what is possible.

One concern I have had is that by starving Ph.D. programs of talent, and by reallocating a lot of this talent to scale-oriented work (as opposed to fundamental research), we could actually push out the AGI timeline. As I noted in a previous blog post, âcorporate politics tends to favor in vogue, consensus ideas over more radical, unpopular ones â the very kinds of ideas that can take years to prove worthwhile, and which scientific breakthroughs often depend on.â Flapping Airplanes is explicitly intended to provide a Ph.D.-like experience â true research independence, long-time horizons â while bridging the pay gap between academia and Major Tech.

One of the biggest learnings of the last decade in AI is the dramatic economic value of fundamental scientific progress. Since academia seems ill-suited to compete with Big Tech on this dimension right now, especially in AI, Flapping Airplanes is taking this into their own hands. And they are focused on precisely the problem that is likely to define the next wave of AI: building models inspired by the data efficiency of biology. With that as a north star, the manufacturer will make bets in a variety of directions to get there.

Sources indicate that there are two coherent motives right now in AI. One is the profit motive, and this should inspire all application builders, given the tremendous opportunity ahead. As I have noted on many occasions, AI is so underpenetrated relative to the capability set available, it is likely to create a golden age for builders for many years to come. There is a large profit pool available, and we are in the very earliest stages of generating it.

Industry observers note that the second coherent motive in AI is AGI, predicated on the belief that now that weâve unlocked a machine intelligence, we should push toward upleveling that intelligence. Economically, progress in this direction is likely to be extremely valuable. The question is how to take on this objective in an efficient way, with a reasonable probability that resources invested will translate into long-term positive results. Flapping Airplanes is a pure play in that direction.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most attractive aspects for me in partnering with Flapping Airplanes was the team. I have met nearly every candidate that has interviewed at Flapping Airplanes, and certainly every person the company has hired. This is one of the best teams Iâve ever seen assembled at the beginning of such an ambitious journey.

There are two core beliefs that make Flapping Airplanes different for top talent:.

A belief that young people have always unlocked fundamental science in the past (Einstein was 26 during his âMiracle Yearâ).

A conviction that AI research is not a mystical domain for experts, but a domain learnable by anyone that is smart and ambitious.

Recent findings suggest that with just these two premises, Flapping Airplanes is at odds with a prestige-obsessed culture in the Valley right now. It is exactly this obsession with substance and with raw individual talent that made Ben so successful at Prod, and it is this âflame spottingâ ability that gives me confidence in the courageous effort that is now Flapping Airplanes.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.
  • Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.
  • In the Prod community, they talk about founders as âtime travelersâ rather than visionaries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.

Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.

In the Prod community, they talk about founders as âtime travelersâ rather than visionaries. Founders donât see the future, they teleport there.

Recent findings suggest that I think this is true in more ways than first meets the eye. To extend the analogy of a chess game (which I recently used in an essay on the AI race and which Will Manidis also articulated beautifully in his essay on âEndgame Playâ), outside observers see startups as temporally sequential, with a beginning (inception/ seed stage), middle (product-market fit/ growth stage), and end (IPO/ scale-up). However, the best founders actually live in all three of these phases simultaneously.

Recent findings suggest that opening: The opening phase of a startup involves the âmagicâ of transforming from a few people with an idea into a âstartup.â Silicon Valley excels at this magic, and Paul Graham is the prophet of the opening. There are many opening strategies, but the lean startup model has proven itself to be the most repeatable one. The ecosystem around manufacturer formation is important because foundational decisions made at this stage are difficult to change later, and so wisdom pays dividends.

Recent findings suggest that midgame: The midgame of a startup begins once product-market fit has been reached. Many startups fail before ever reaching this stage. Product-market fit requires deeply understanding a customerâs need, and building a solution. Once product-market fit has been reached, you need to build a company â figure out how to hire people, manage people, and improve the product. You need to achieve some type of takeoff, forward momentum that will allow the business to grow from something tiny and irrelevant into something meaningful and important. Board members exist to transmit inter-generational knowledge on midgame play. Since the nature of the midgame is always evolving, founders need to filter this through their own prism to arrive at truth.

Endgame: The endgame of a startup is the infinite future â itâs never really reached. The endgame is important, because without a vision of the future, the present has very little value â see the recent SaaSpocalypse. Elon Musk is the prophet of the endgame, he has always focused on the hardest problems, knowing that ambitious problems attract excellent people and unleash them to do their best work.

According to recent reports, some startups seem uniquely engineered for the opening, some for the midgame, and some for the endgame. A hot AI firm from Stanford students is engineered for the opening game â they will easily be able to recruit friends and a bike ride to Sand Hill road easily yields capital. A vertical SaaS company is engineered for the midgame â getting off the ground is hard and recruiting the early team is challenging, but once you unlock PMF, thereâs a clear path for how to scale it up. And a deep tech company is engineered for the endgame, itâs always clear from the moment of inception why that company should pass the âwho cares?â test.

Every startup has a different set of challenges depending on what parts of the game are structurally easier and harder. For example, a startup with a weak endgame story will struggle to raise funding without immense traction. A startup with a strong opening story is at risk of hubris, employees thinking the company has reached the promised land, when nothing substantial has been achieved. And the âvalley of deathâ is famous in deep tech, precisely because a strong endgame story is always preceded by a long, fatigued midgame. The #1 piece of advice I give friends who are starting companies is to be aware of these biases, and explicitly combat them.

Sources indicate that what is so incredible about the best companies, and the best founders, is that they appear to be playing the opening, midgame and endgame simultaneously. In the best companies, it is always early days and there is a big dream ahead (the opening vibe), even many years in. This is how Clay feels, even though the organization is almost ten years old. Similarly, the best startups often have midgame characteristics at the opening â within a few months, they can show traction and improvement, creating a sense of forward momentum. For example, RunwayMLâs incredible open-source growth, years before Stable Diffusion. And finally, the best companies create a feeling of inevitability early, such that employees genuinely feel like they are moving the world forward. For example, Anduril pioneering modern defense tech.

One phrase Iâve often used to describe the best founders is, âNo matter what happens, they are going to win.â Alex Wangâs incredible journey at Scale from strength to strength was an early and illustrative example of this concept for me. The journey of Crusoe from crypto miner to AI factory builder is another great story of grit and judgement. What has crystalized for me now is seeing a superstructure that makes this possible â these founders are constantly holding the opening, midgame and endgame in their minds at the same time, and hence they are able to create a flexible, nimble culture that is always reinventing itself, and they are much quicker in adjusting their business strategy when the times are changing.

My advice to founders is therefore this: No matter where you are in your journey, donât think about your business sequentially. Force yourself to play all three games at once â when planning product decisions, when making hires, when pitching investors. If you are in the midgame, you still need to care about opening style hires that could change the business. If you are in the opening, you need to think about the endgame, because thatâs what will inspire others to join you and help turn your vision into reality. And if you are in the endgame, you should still care about midgame momentum and opening creativity â thatâs how you will become absolutely massive. As you build your manufacturer, each of these narratives should be getting stronger â you canât just focus on the one that seems immediately in front of you.

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1548 w)

Oobah Butler Can Sell You Anything—If You’re a Rich Idiot

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1548 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You’d think that Oobah Butler would have run out of schemes by now.
  • The gonzo British documentarian’s repertoire includes creating an entirely fake restaurant—The Shed at Dulwich—and getting it to the top spot on London’s Tripadvisor; selling bottles of Amazon drivers’ urine on the ecommerce site; and convincing venture capitalists to give him $1 million.
  • But as his new HBO show, Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow, makes perfectly clear, Butler still has plenty of tricks up his sleeve—and it’s a delight to watch them unfold.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’d think that Oobah Butler would have run out of schemes by now.

The gonzo British documentarian’s repertoire includes creating an entirely fake restaurant—The Shed at Dulwich—and getting it to the top spot on London’s Tripadvisor; selling bottles of Amazon drivers’ urine on the ecommerce site; and convincing venture capitalists to give him $1 million.

But as his new HBO show, Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow, makes perfectly clear, Butler still has plenty of tricks up his sleeve—and it’s a delight to watch them unfold.

The series releases November 22. Each of the premier season’s five episodes centers on Butler scamming his way into success in a different industry—wellness, wine, dating, music, and a finale I do not want to spoil—with increasingly outlandish ideas that, somehow, almost no one advises him against.

His shock of bleach-blond hair and appearance of a Victorian ghost notwithstanding, there are undeniable similarities between Butler’s style and that of master of manipulation Nathan Fielder. Both use satire and parody to make social commentaries, and both often divert from their original plans by hyperfocusing on what the average person might consider a tangential detail, carrying these side quests to extreme lengths. But while Fielder has sometimes been criticized for roping unassuming working-class folks into his hijinks, in Butler’s case the joke is almost always on the rich and powerful—and the systems that allow them to prevail.

Butler in the Upcoming York weather.

“The whole show can be reduced to ‘monkey see, monkey do,’” Butler tells me from a coffee shop at the Upcoming York Historical Society in Manhattan, where he’s just ordered a latte with four espresso shots and been recognized from TikTok by a fellow patron. “I just find these bad actors and copy them.”.

Butler’s knack for convincing high-profile—in some cases notorious—executives and tastemakers to appear on camera and earnestly weigh in on his ridiculous intends at times boggles the mind. In the series premiere, he sets out to start a wellness firm that sells the tears of human children as a skin serum, and gets none other than former Theranos chief creative officer Patrick O’Neill to consult on a marketing strategy.

Applying his characteristic charm, Butler tells O’Neill he “smashed it” with creating mystique around the scandal-plagued biotech startup, to which O’Neill replies, “Thank you, yeah. I think it’s good to share the knowledge.”.

Butler wearing glasses designed to collect the tears of children.

After briefly expressing hesitancy around the ethical sourcing of the tears, O’Neill begins offering Butler packaging advice: a tear-shaped bottle, and the two discuss the name Lacrimé (“tears” in Italian). “It makes it feel exotic and not necessarily something you’d see from Johnson and Johnson,” O’Neill says, in all seriousness.

Confiding in $1,500-an-hour lawyer Jennifer Keller about how he may have committed fraud with his wellness venture, Butler tells her the industry is “a gold rush of bullshit. And I want in.” She laughs and indicates that he sounds “more and more like an American.” It’s all very funny, but as the name of the show hints, there is a Robin Hood quality to Butler’s scamming, in this case exposing the poorly regulated nature of skin care and supplements.

Butler has chosen the New York Historical Society as our meeting point because he loves history, and New York’s in particular. When he first moved here in February 2024, he started reading Robert Caro’s The Power Broker, a biography of influential urban planner Robert Moses, giving him an understanding of “how power works” in the city. But his itch to move came well before that, when he visited in 2016.

“I just found it so inspiring,” he says, dressed in a maroon velvet shirt, baggy dark jeans, and Salomon sneakers, a Patagonia backpack slung over his shoulders, as we set out for a walk in Central Park. “I got to an age where I just thought, well if I don’t do this now, I probably am not going to do it.”.

Although Newly introduced York is indeed full of power brokers—and very wealthy ones at that—he says it’s different from the aristocracy he grew up around in Feckenham, a 700-person “Hobbiton-style village” in the UK.

“I grew up in a lower-class family … I’ve definitely got a bit of a chip on my shoulder about class,” he says, noting that he’s the youngest of six siblings. “And America, for all of its problems, there is something amazing about how I see the same guys who really wind me up in the UK—upper-class kind of guys—and the way that they walk the earth and the way they feel and the way they carry themselves. I see them come here and no one gives a shit. Really, truly, no one gives a shit.”.

In a recent development, butler didn't go to college. He started a band called My Grey Horse in 2010, playing guitar and singing. Around the age of 17, he began writing music reviews, secretly hoping to score his band some coverage. “It was a scam on the go,” he indicates. But he caught the writing bug, finding it “meditative.” Later, he joined VICE (where I previously worked as a senior reporter) as a freelance video host, making a bunch of documentaries, including the extremely viral one about The Shed. From there, he did several films for the UK’s Channel 4 and cohosted MTV’s Catfish UK.

“It changed my life and was absolutely the right thing to do. I wouldn't have been able to afford to move here if I hadn't done Catfish,” he claims.

According to recent reports, though he tells me he’s not a comedian, Butler is a natural clown, and at times even just his buffoonish mannerisms are enough to elicit laughs. Maybe he’s such a natural because he comes from a long line of schemers. He tells me his great grandfather moved to the US in the late 19th century as part of the fur trade, but he would also sell rabbit droppings rolled in flour as medicine.

“I'm cut from a line of people who sell shit,” he notes.

Industry observers note that though he may not have firsthand experiences, Butler’s perceptions of hoity-toity cultural institutions—and their vulnerabilities—are spot on. In an episode about fine wine, he embarks on a mission to sell a smoke-tainted swill brand called Fumare as a high-end product—even though it would normally be tossed by wine producers or used for barbecue sauces. Part of his task is to convince New York Times wine critic Eric Asimov to give the smoked wine a good review.

Industry observers note that butler creates a psychological profile of Asimov, determining that he’s a “contrarian” who “wants to be romanced.” Knowing he’s a fan of Bob Dylan, Butler just happens to be playing a Dylan song on the piano when Asimov shows up for a tasting. While Asimov pans the first glass of smoky wine, Butler tries again, by pretending it's actually a glass of Barolo, the same stuff Asimov says he fell in love with when he first got into wine. “I have no complaints,” Asimov says—an endorsement that Butler promptly attaches to Fumare’s label.

In another episode, Butler starts an AI dating organization called Sole, but instead of matching people with a chatbot, as he’s purporting to do, he matches them with other humans to see if they connect.

“The idea was that people trust in the technology more than a conversation with one another,” he says.

These days, many of Butler’s stunts either directly or indirectly relate to Big Tech—for good reason.

According to recent reports, “A lot of it is built on speculative promises and the idea of utopia rather than connected to reality. Tech CEOs constantly coming out and lying about what they’ll be able to do in 10 years to shit-coin their stock price,” he claims, adding that the sector is “riddled with inauthenticity.”.

Sources indicate that despite having the backing of HBO, his own work still feels authentic and haphazard, as opposed to overly polished. He states it’s usually just him and a couple of other people carrying out the stunts. “One of the episodes was basically me and me in my bedroom,” he says, noting that while he’s been working on the finale for six years, originally envisioning it as a feature film, all the others except for the pilot were shot in the last eight months.

“There’s a DIY characteristic to the stuff anyway, and I want the people watching to not feel excluded from the pieces of it. And that's always a thing where I'm like, ‘Oh, if the budget for the show was much bigger, it might not feel like this anymore,’” he tells me.

Considering all the pranks he’s pulled off, I ask him point-blank if it’s a bad idea for people to answer the phone when he calls. He rebuffs, pressing me for my take.

Truthfully, I think there’s a high chance that if you engage with Butler on camera, you’ll come off looking like a fool—particularly if you’re someone with any type of clout. But for the sake of my own entertainment, I hope people keep doing it.

They knew there had to be a better wayâand with Firetiger, theyâve built exactly that.

#3108. Are Smart Car Seats Worth It? I Tested Two to Find Out (2026)

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1544 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Are Smart Car Seats Worth It? I Tested Two to Find Out (2026)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1544 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that car seats had some pretty humble beginnings.
  • It has been revealed that many car seat manufacturers are adding technology to, for lack of a better term, give parents a second set of eyes.
  • According to recent reports, it sounds appealing, right?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that car seats had some pretty humble beginnings. Even I, an early-’90s baby, slightly recoil every time I see a picture of myself strapped into a flimsy plastic bucket with a loud geometric-print cover that once held my life in its clutches. Car seat design and safety standards have come a long way, and today’s models are quite souped up, with cup holders, rotating bases, and enough bells and whistles to rival an Escalade. And now, they’re getting smart.

It has been revealed that many car seat manufacturers are adding technology to, for lack of a better term, give parents a second set of eyes. Think Bluetooth-connected chest clips, sensors, apps, and real-time alerts that ping your phone if something goes awry, whether that’s an installation matter or if a chest clip comes unbuckled while the car’s moving.

According to recent reports, it sounds appealing, right? Especially for parents who already have plenty to worry about and are often juggling a million things just to get out the door in the morning. But it’s worth asking: Do these features actually make car seats safer? Or are parents paying for peace of mind?

Sources indicate that I tested two smart car seats, the Babyark Classic ($799) and the Cybex Cloud G Pro ($550), to see if this technology lives up to the hype and whether a smart seat is worth adding to your registry. Because while an app-connected car seat might seem cool and offer some reassurance, no amount of technology can replace proper installation and use. Keep in mind that they’re not exactly apples-to-apples comparisons; the Babyark is a convertible car seat designed to grow with your little one, while the Cybex is an infant carrier. I tested the Babyark with my toddler daughter and the Cybex with my infant son, giving me a chance to see how each one worked at different stages of parenthood. But both offer a glimpse into how companies are integrating technology into car seats, and I wanted to see how they perform in everyday life.

Industry observers note that many smart car seats revolve around sensors. Some come equipped with sensors that help caregivers determine if the seat is installed correctly. Others use Bluetooth-enabled chest clips to send notifications to your phone if the chest clip breaks free mid-ride or if you walk away from your car while your child is still buckled in. A few models even have crash detection, which can send notifications to designated emergency contacts if a collision is detected.

In a recent development, the biggest difference comes down to how the technology is integrated. Some models, like the Cybex I tested, rely on a Bluetooth chest clip that connects to an app. Babyark takes a slightly different approach, with mechanical indicators on its Classic model and a swankier electronic sensor system built into the base of its higher-end Smart and Premium models.

The first thing I noticed about the Babyark out of the box was its base setup, which was different from any other car seats I’ve used. The base is a spaceship-looking device with a fold-out support leg and anti-rebound bar. The seat itself is pretty bulky, but I didn’t mind too much, since by the time I started using it, my daughter was old enough that I didn’t need to haul her around in an infant seat anymore.

Car seat installation can be an exercise in patience, but I found setup pretty straightforward. The Babyark app walked me through every step, with video tutorials for each stage. Once everything was in place, indicators on the base glowed green. (Red means something’s off.).

Recent findings suggest that the app is easy to navigate, but once I installed the seat, I pretty much forgot about it. I enabled notifications in case something needed attention, but in my several months of using the seat, nothing has warranted an alert so far, aside from the occasional random disconnection.

Industry observers note that it’s worth noting that the Babyark offers different versions of the seat, all with different technology. The Classic model, which I have, presently retails at $790 and offers guided installation videos and mechanical indicators. Babyark's Smart and Premium models—which retail for $999 and $1,190, respectively—add features like forgotten child alerts and impact detection. That’s a roughly $200 to $400 jump, which is worth considering if you’re particularly interested in those features.

You can check the app for basic statistics, like how much time your child spends in the seat, but I haven’t felt the need to follow this closely. More importantly, I didn’t find myself opening the app to monitor the seat while my daughter was in it. At the end of the day, the Babyark feels like a regular car seat to me. But a great, sturdy car seat at that!

Sources indicate that I also tried out the Cloud G Pro, which comes with SensorSafe, a Bluetooth chest clip that communicates with the Cybex app on your phone. Pairing the clip, which looks and functions like any other, with my phone was easy peasy. When I intentionally tested the alerts, they worked as expected and came through almost immediately.

It has been revealed that the temperature notifications worked, but almost too well. SensorSafe sends an alert when your car’s interior climbs to above 95 degrees Fahrenheit or drops below 45. Depending on the weather, your car might already be outside that range when you first get in, and it takes a little time for the cabin to warm up or cool down. So don’t be surprised if you get an alert before the AC or heat has a chance to do its thing.

It has been revealed that sensorSafe can also alert you if the clip becomes unbuckled while driving or if you leave your child buckled in the seat and walk away with your phone. In the latter scenario, the default setting has your phone loudly announce “CHILD IN CAR!” in a man’s deep voice, which scared the hoots out of me the first time it went off. If you don’t respond to the alert (you can stop or snooze it), the app will notify your emergency contact and share your location.

In a recent development, like the Babyark, I didn’t find myself opening the Cybex app very often to check on things. I mostly let it run in the background and waited for notifications rather than actively checking in on the system. The alerts worked just fine, but I used the app so infrequently that my phone eventually offloaded it.

It has been revealed that as appealing as all those gadgets and gizmos sound, car seats aren’t foolproof. “These are supplements. They're not substitutes,” indicates Jennifer Booge, a car seat safety expert with the National Safety Council. “We have to make sure that we're understanding how to use the car seat correctly, because there is so much to know, and every car seat is so different.”.

According to data collected through the NSC’s National Digital Car Seat Check Form, a little over 72 percent of car seats entered into the system have some form of misuse. Manufacturers are working to address these complications with installation videos and app-based guidance, but Booge states there’s still not enough research to determine whether smart features actually improve safety.

According to recent reports, some car seat manufacturers offer access to certified child passenger safety technicians who can walk you through installation questions. I experienced this firsthand with the Babyark. Even after following the app’s instructions and getting the green light that everything was secure, I still had some reservations about how much the seat was wiggling. I reached out to the manufacturer, and they virtually walked me through the installation. (Which turned out to be correct; car seats are supposed to have a slight wiggle, no more than an inch back and forth.).

“Don't be afraid to pick up the phone and call or schedule that virtual appointment and meet with those experts that are there to help you, because it's not easy,” Booge notes. “Every car seat is different. Every vehicle and car seat combination is different.”.

As Booge points out, tech can be useful even when it isn’t built into the seat itself. The rise of virtual appointments gives caregivers access to certified technicians that they may not otherwise have available. At the end of the day, a car seat doesn’t need a battery or an app to do its job, and all the technology in the world can’t replace knowing how to use it properly.

It has been revealed that do you need a smart car seat? Probably not. After testing the Babyark and the Cybex Cloud G Pro with SensorSafe, I’m not totally convinced the added tech is worth paying a premium for. Both offered features I appreciated, and they certainly gave me peace of mind, but neither fundamentally changed how I use a car seat day to day. I’d rather prioritize a seat that fits my child and my vehicle, and that I can use correctly, rather than pay extra for an app I rarely open. All in all, my biggest takeaway is not to mistake more features for more safety.

Services: The New Software

📅 05 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The next $1T company will be a software company masquerading as a services firm.
  • In a recent development, every founder building an AI tool is asking the same question: what happens when the next version of Claude makes my product a feature?
  • Writing code is mostly intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The next $1T company will be a software company masquerading as a services firm.

In a recent development, every founder building an AI tool is asking the same question: what happens when the next version of Claude makes my product a feature? Theyâre right to worry. If you sell the tool, youâre in a race against the model. But if you sell the work, every improvement in the model makes your service faster, cheaper, and harder to compete with. A firm might spend $10K a year for QuickBooks and $120K on an accountant to close the books. The next legendary company will just close the books.

Writing code is mostly intelligence. Knowing what to build next is judgement.

Translating a spec into code, testing, debugging: the rules are complex but they are rules. Judgement is different. It requires experience and taste, instinct built on years of practice. Deciding which feature to build next, whether to take on tech debt, when to ship before itâs ready.

Industry observers note that A year ago, most Cursor owners treated AI as autocomplete. Today, more tasks are started by agents than by humans. Software engineering accounts for over half of all AI tool usage across professions. Every other category is still in single digits. The reason is that software engineering is primarily intelligence work. AI has crossed the threshold where it can do most of the intelligence work autonomously and leave the judgement to humans. Software engineering got there first. It is coming to every single profession.

Sources indicate that A copilot sells the tool. An autopilot sells the work.

Sources indicate that until recently, AI models were still developing intelligence and judgement, so the right approach was to build a copilot first: put AI in the hands of a professional and let them decide what to do with it. Harvey sells to law firms. Rogo sells to investment banks. The professional is the customer, the tool makes them more productive, and they take responsibility for the output.

In a recent development, today, the models are intelligent enough that in some categories the best place to start is as an autopilot. Crosby sells to the manufacturer that needs an NDA drafted, not to outside counsel. WithCoverage sells to the CFO who needs insurance, not to the broker. The customer is buying the outcome directly. The work budget in any profession dwarfs the tool budget, and autopilots capture the work budget from day one.

The higher the intelligence ratio in any field, the sooner autopilots will win.

Todayâs judgement will become tomorrowâs intelligence. As AI systems accumulate proprietary data about what good judgement looks like in their domain, the frontier will shift. Copilots and autopilots will converge. The copilot-to-autopilot transition has already begun in several categories. But the starting position matters because it determines where autopilots can win customers now and begin compounding the data that will eventually let them handle judgement too.

The Autopilot Playbook: Outsourcing as the Wedge.

For every dollar spent on software, six are spent on services.

Sources indicate that the total addressable market for autopilots is all labour spend in a category, insourced and outsourced combined. But the right place to start is where outsourcing already exists.

If a task is already outsourced, it tells you three things. One, the company has accepted that this work can be done externally. Two, thereâs an existing budget line that can be substituted cleanly. Three, the buyer is already purchasing an outcome. Replacing an outsourcing contract with an AI-native services provider is a vendor swap. Replacing headcount is a reorg.

The playbook: companies should start with the outsourced, intelligence-heavy task. Nail distribution. Expand toward the insourced, judgement-heavy work as the AI compounds. The outsourced task is the wedge. The insourced work is the long-term TAM.

Crosby started with NDAs: a well-defined task, primarily intelligence, that most companies already outsource to external counsel. The budget exists, the scope is clear, the ROI is immediate, and the substitution is frictionless.

Plotting every services vertical on an intelligence-to-judgement spectrum and outsourced-to-insourced ratio produces a priority map with labour TAM in brackets. The list is illustrative.

In a recent development, insurance brokerage ($140-200B). The largest dollar market on this list. Standard commercial lines are highly standardised: the brokerâs value-add is essentially shopping across carriers and filling forms, pure intelligence work. The distribution layer is incredibly fragmented, tens of thousands of small brokers each running the same process, so no single incumbent controls the customer relationship. WithCoverage and Harper are interesting newcomers.

Sources indicate that accounting and audit ($50-80B outsourced in the US alone). The US has lost roughly 340,000 accountants over five years while demand has grown. 75% of CPAs are nearing retirement, the licensing path is long, and starting salaries lag tech and finance. That structural shortage is pushing firms to accept AI faster than almost any other profession. Rillet is building the AI-native ERP that will close the books. Basis started as a copilot for accountants.

Industry observers note that healthcare revenue cycle ($50-80B outsourced in US). People hear âhealthcareâ and assume itâs judgement-heavy, but the billing layer is almost pure intelligence. Medical coding is translating clinical notes into ~70,000 standardised ICD-10 codes. The rules are complex but they are rules. The outsourcing is already mature and outcome-based. An autopilot just has to do the same thing at lower cost. Anterior is the furthest along.

Sources indicate that claims adjusting ($50-80B including TPAs). On the other side of the insurance policy, claims adjusting is a separate autopilot surface. Standard-line claims are settled by interpreting policy language against damage schedules and setting reserves using actuarial tables. The adjuster workforce is aging out and nobodyâs replacing them. The market is massively outsourced to independents and TPAs like Crawford and Sedgwick. One industry, at least two distinct autopilot opportunities. Pace is building the autopilot for claims handling. Strala is building an AI-native TPA.

Tax advisory ($30-35B). CPA licensing creates a regulatory moat, but 80-90% of the underlying work is intelligence. Every additional jurisdiction a tax autopilot handles deepens its data moat. Multi-jurisdiction complexity is exactly what SMBs outsource because no single in-house accountant can cover it. TaxGPT is an early mover alongside Skalar and Ravical in Europe.

In a recent development, legal, transactional work ($20-25B). Contract drafting, NDAs, regulatory filings: high intelligence, routinely outsourced. The work product is standardised enough that quality is verifiable, so the buyer can trust AI output without deep legal expertise. Harvey is the emerging leader and is moving quickly to autopilot; Crosby and Lawhive are the autopilot-native newcomers.

IT managed services ($100B+). Every SMB outsources its IT. Patching, monitoring, user provisioning, alert triage: intelligence work running on repeat across thousands of identical environments. The existing software layer (ConnectWise, Datto) sells tools to the MSP. Nobody has yet sold âyour IT runsâ directly to the organization as an outcome. Edra is automating IT processes. Serval is automating IT support.

Supply chain and procurement ($200B+). Most enterprises negotiate seriously with only their top 20% of suppliers. The long tail gets zero attention because itâs not economical to have humans do the work. Contract leakage runs 2-5% of total procurement spend. The wedge is abandoned work: no budget line to justify, no incumbent to displace, just found money. Magentic is building the AI for direct procurement, AskLio for indirect procurement. Tacto is building both the system of record and copilot for the midmarket.

Industry observers note that recruitment and staffing ($200B+). The largest services market on this list. The top of the hiring funnel (screening, matching, outreach) is pure intelligence, but closing a candidate and assessing culture fit is judgement built on years of pattern recognition. The autopilot wedge exists in high-volume, low-judgement roles where matching is standardised. Juicebox, Mercor, Jack & Jill are emerging leaders building across the spectrum.

Management consulting ($300-400B). Huge market but the work is mostly judgement. The interesting question is whether AI can disaggregate consulting into intelligence components (data gathering, benchmarking) and judgement components (strategic recommendations), with the intelligence layer getting automated and the judgement layer staying human. Best candidates TBD.

In a recent development, in 2025, the fastest-growing AI companies were copilots. In 2026, many will try to become autopilots. They have the product and the customer knowledge. But they also face the innovatorâs dilemma: selling the work means cutting their own customers out of doing it. Thatâs the opening for pure-play autopilots.

If youâre building one, reach out. julien@sequoiacap.com / @julienbek.

#3103. Tesla’s Cybercab Is the Subscription Hell They Told You Not to Worry About

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (912 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla’s Cybercab Is the Subscription Hell They Told You Not to Worry About

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (912 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Or in the case of Tesla’s self-driving Cybercab, several.
  • According to recent reports, last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs.
  • From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is always a catch. Or in the case of Tesla’s self-driving Cybercab, several.

According to recent reports, last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet's Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox, offer self-driving rides on ride-hail networks, but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s "limited release” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December.

From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.

The business model raises questions about what people will actually get when they buy a Cybercab. “You’ll never really own the car,” says Ivan Drury, the director of insights at Edmunds. “It’s more like $30,000 to buy into a franchise.”.

According to documents posted on Tesla’s website, the vehicle “will not operate” without what Tesla is calling an “autonomy subscription," a monthly fee that will start at $299. If owners don’t pay on time and in full, their self-driving cars won’t work. If they try to operate the vehicles in areas that don’t support the service—right now, they’re restricted to portions of cities in Florida and Texas—their self-driving cars won’t work. (That area can expand, contract, or “relocate” at any time.).

Sources indicate that if owners do anything that Tesla deems "unauthorized or inappropriate," the company says it can suspend or cancel the subscription—and their self-driving cars won’t work. If the vehicle loses connectivity, the self-driving cars won’t work. (“Tesla is not responsible for carrier, spectrum, environmental, or other external outages,” its “autonomy agreement” says.).

Tesla also reserves the right to make an owner’s car not work at any time: It says it can, for any safety or security purpose, suspend or terminate access to Cybercab tech, or restrict operations by location, road type, weather, or “condition.” This is particularly salient because the Cybercab is also under investigation by US safety regulators, who are trying to understand why Tesla believes the vehicle meets safety standards without so many of the parts and systems required.

Tesla didn’t respond to a request for comment.

It has been revealed that for years, automakers have seen increasingly software-dominated vehicles as an opportunity to get drivers hooked on the same special sauce that makes Netflix, Amazon, and Spotify so potent: monthly subscription services. Because these vehicles can receive over-the-air software updates, manufacturers can offer drivers upcoming services as they make them. The upside is high, tech-style margins that keep rolling in, versus the razor-thin ones seen in car-making. A 2024 report suggested that connected-car features could one day be a $200 billion industry.

In some ways, the subscription model is working. Today, some automakers charge extra for remote start, security, internet connectivity, and advanced driver assistance features. General Motors mentioned it made $2.7 billion in subscription-related revenue last year from fees drivers paid for its OnStar and Super Cruise services.

But some customers have also found the business model yucky, or even offensive. Why charge extra to “unlock” a feature that’s already built into a car? If an automaker can add a fresh feature at any time, can’t they also take it away? And if they can take it away, what does "ownership" mean? In 2022, BMW told drivers in select countries it would activate factory-installed heated seats for a monthly or one-time fee; it eventually backed down after public outcry, pledging the company would no longer charge subscription fees for pre-installed hardware. (BMW is still pursuing a subscription model for some features.) “Consumers hate being nickel-and-dimed for subscriptions,” states Drury.

Sources indicate that tesla was an early mover in the subscription feature space and has offered connectivity and driver-assistance features for monthly or one-time fees for a decade. As the organization has shifted away from making cars and toward robotics and autonomous vehicles, executives have made clear that charging for services is the future. (Its Robotaxi service at the moment picks up fare-paying passengers in parts of eight US cities.) So Tesla buyers may be particularly amenable to paying monthly to make their self-driving cars go.

In a recent development, in exchange for monthly fees, buyers will also get access to other services, too, including remote support, roadside assistance, tire, air filter, and windshield wiper replacements, and tire and camera inspections. (The agreement says that list might change, too.) Cybercabs will be able to “travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center,” the manufacturer says. The fee doesn't cover insurance.

Cybercab buyers will have other restrictions. The vehicle is for personal use only. Even though CEO Elon Musk has repeatedly said owners will be able to put their vehicles on Tesla’s wider Robotaxi network to make money during downtime, and even has an online interest form for those who want to own and operate their own Cybercab fleets, the current ownership agreement prohibits that. Buyers are also prohibited from selling or transferring their vehicles without Tesla’s written consent. The company “advises against” children under 13 riding in the Cybercab, and prohibits children from riding without an adult present.

In a post on X, Musk showed no apparent compunction about the Cybercab business model, but did say the monthly price for autonomy “is too high.” He wrote that the price should be “more like ~$115/month.”.

Cliff and Steven are making petabytes of security data searchable in seconds, and opening the door to a new era of AI-driven security operations.

Awhile back, I was deep in research on the next generation of security infrastructure, talking to CISOs and security engineers at some of the most technically sophisticated companies in Silicon Valley. I asked them all the same question Iâd asked a decade earlier when I worked in enterprise software: Whatâs your biggest headache? The consistency of their answers surprised me. âWe drown in logs we canât afford to keep,â as one security leader put it, âand go blind on the logs we canât afford to search.â.

Enterprise security today is a story of impossible choices. The tools that teams rely on generate enormous amounts of log dataâevery API call, every login event, every network connection. To investigate cyber threats, they need all of it, often going back a year or more. But storing everything in a SIEM like Splunk is prohibitively expensive; costs could easily consume 15% of a CISOâs entire budget. Instead, companies make a compromise: they keep only the most recent 10 to 30 days of logs in their SIEM and park the rest in Amazon S3, where storage is cheap, but the data is effectively frozen. When a breach, a compliance audit, or a forensic investigation happens, security teams discover too late that the evidence they need is out of reach, opaque and unsearchable.

I first heard about Scanner from a member of the security team at Temporal, one of our portfolio companies, who called it, âcrazy fast.â I looked into it, and reached out to Cliff Crosland right away.

What Cliff and his co-founder Steven Wu have built is elegant in its insight. They asked: what would a log search engine look like if you designed it from scratch for object storage? The answer was a purpose-built inverted index that maps field values directly to file regions in S3. Rather than combing through billions of rows, Scanner narrows each query to only the relevant slices of data. A petabyte of logs becomes interactive. Queries that took hours now run in seconds. And a streaming detection engine runs hundreds of detection rules continuously across tens of terabytes a day, without re-scanning the world for each one.

Cliff and Steven are exactly the kind of founders we look for. Both Stanford CS alums, they were engineering leads together at Accompany (acquired by Cisco), where they built core data infrastructure under demanding, production-scale conditions. They have an obsession with performance that borders on the philosophical; they donât tolerate systems that feel slow. And they have the expertise to build something better.

Whatâs most striking about Scanner isnât the technologyâthough that is genuinely impressive. Itâs the customers. The companies using Scanner today read like a whoâs who of the cloud native world: Notion, Ramp, Benchling, Confluent, Lemonade, BeyondTrust. And theyâre not just using itâthey love it. Benchling replaced another product after a forced tenfold price increase, and their head of security engineering called it one of the best technical decisions their team had made. Ramp started with security logs and then expanded to application logs, reducing their SIEM bill in the process. Notionâs detection and response team built an internal AI agent that autonomously runs security investigations using Scanner.

That last example signals whatâs to come. We are entering a new era of security operations, where AI agents will do much of the investigative work that today consumes hours of human time. But agents need to rapidly iterate, ask questions and follow threads; queries canât take minutes, much less hours. Scannerâs speed is enabling these agentic security workflows across a wide range of companies: within weeks of their MCP release, nearly a third of Scannerâs customers were already using it in production, and agents now account for 80% of queries on the platform. That is not a prototype or a promising beta. That is the future arriving ahead of schedule.

Sequoia is proud to lead Scannerâs Series A, and weâre thrilled to partner with Cliff, Steven and their team as they work to transform a market overdue for reinvention. Scanner is winning hearts and minds among the most technically forward organizations today, and together, they will define the next decade of security infrastructure.

Breaking: AI Told These Ex-Google Guys How to Build a Billion-Dollar Weapons Business

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1156 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED
