💡 Key Takeaways
  • For our inaugural WIRED Yearbook, we celebrate the people, inventions, and viral moments that made it a little more bearable—and are already defining the future.
  • ANIMATIONS BY LUKTHIS STUDIO ILLUSTRATIONS AND PHOTO TREATMENT BY ROB VARGAS.
  • Surveillance at every traffic light.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For our inaugural WIRED Yearbook, we celebrate the people, inventions, and viral moments that made it a little more bearable—and are already defining the future.

ANIMATIONS BY LUKTHIS STUDIO ILLUSTRATIONS AND PHOTO TREATMENT BY ROB VARGAS.

An internet devoured by AI. Surveillance at every traffic light. Global leaders who seem determined to bring about dystopia. At the end of a year like 2026, it’s tempting to conclude that there’s little room for idealism. Don’t give in! After all, this year we also saw a latest generation of filmmakers challenge Hollywood, teenagers take on AI companies, and scientists make once-unimaginable breakthroughs. We saw activists fight surveillance, astronauts do the impossible, and an adorable raccoon melt the internet’s black heart. So for the first time, we’re publishing a WIRED Yearbook: our very subjective, occasionally ridiculous, always enthusiastic collection of the people, institutions, inventions, and moments that offered optimism in 2026. I hope it gives you a healthy kick of bullishness—and the vigor to keep fighting for the future you want to see.

—Katie Drummond, Global Editorial Director.

From the ecstatic night the Knicks won the NBA championship to the surprising ease with which Newly introduced York absorbed the chaos of the World Cup to the record-low violent crime—it’s been a huge 2026 for the greatest city in the world. WIRED first sat down with Zohran Mamdani in 2025, when he was still just a candidate for mayor. A year later, as the midterm elections loomed, we returned.

KATIE DRUMMOND: We talked last year about social media as a tool for campaigning. How are you thinking about social media now as a tool for governance?

Sources indicate that ZOHRAN MAMDANI: You have to continue to recognize the fact that for many New Yorkers, this is how they engage with the world. It is yet another medium that has to be treated with the same legitimacy and respect as traditional mediums.

What’s your point of view on the data center movement? Why do you think that specific issue has become such a flash point?

The movement to oppose data centers is one that gives me a real sense of hope.

Sources indicate that it’s a bipartisan fight. What you’re seeing from Americans across the country is an opposition to what these data centers would mean for their day-to-day lives, what they would mean for their electricity rates, what they would mean for the environment. It’s also a repudiation of what has been governing politics for the last few years when it comes to AI, which is: Our risk, their reward.

You worry that we’re in a bubble?

You worry that bubble’s gonna pop?

Sources indicate that last year I asked you if technology was making democracy stronger or weaker. You said weaker. What about today?

Industry observers note that I have family members sending me AI videos of me, thinking that they’re real. One complimented me on a 45-minute debate that I had with a European member of parliament. I was like, “This is not me.” There is a real crisis of faith as to what is real right now.

What do you hope the Democratic party looks like in, say, 2036?

I hope that party looks like one that realizes the only majority in this country is the working class, and fights for it. An ambitious version of the party cannot only be one that we find in history books. We need that to be a living, breathing politic. The people who run it have to be the American people.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

In early August, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez confirmed that she was freezing her eggs. “Usually I keep my private life quite private,” she mentioned in an Instagram video, before opening up about the process and sharing videos of the self-administered hormone injections.

This wasn’t an extraordinary event—more women than ever are making the same decision—but the internet exploded anyway. “This desire to start having children late in life is completely baffling to me,” wrote the far-right commentator Matt Walsh on X. “Totally backwards and ridiculous.”.

Republicans weren’t all on the same page: Katie Miller, wife of the man recently promoted to White House chief of staff, defended AOC, writing on X, “If one woman wants to preserve her right to have children, which means more than having none—we should celebrate that.”.

Industry observers note that it is true that the Republican party has been intensely focused on women’s fertility. The expectation of motherhood, along with the proliferation of pro-natalism, has become core to the party. For conservative commentators to bash the New York representative felt incongruous at best. The White House itself reportedly didn’t love Walsh’s take.

Meanwhile, in an interview with ABC, Ocasio-Cortez remarked it was vital to “normalize” the procedure at a time when “this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country.”.

In a recent development, as the 37-year-old congresswoman considers a presidential run in 2028, expect more of this. Conversations about her body, her health, and her possible maternal well-being will be front and center no matter what. She could have 100 children, and Republicans would spend time complaining about their names. —Leah Feiger.

Australia restricted children’s access to social media at the end of 2025, and 2026 saw several other countries follow suit. Brazil banned features such as infinite scroll and autoplaying videos, also mandating more adult supervision and age checks. The European Union announced plans to prevent under-13s from using both social media and AI chatbots.

The jury’s still out on whether these bans actually work, but speaking of juries, let’s talk about Meta. After being accused of harming the brains of youngs everywhere, the tech giant paid an $18 billion settlement, agreeing to new features like late-night restrictions and parental controls. “I’m proud of both the work Meta has done to protect kids historically and of this new groundbreaking agreement,” noted the firm’s chief legal officer, lamely. If bans don’t work, lawsuits might. —Isabella Ward.

Industry observers note that since October 2025, Bari Weiss, a longtime opinion journalist with no experience running a large organization, has been the editor in chief of CBS News. In that role, she has operated on a theory that has informed much of her career: People want common sense; her views (broadly, that the Israeli government is good and wokes are bad) are common sense; therefore, people want her views.

It doesn’t look good. In January, Weiss tapped anchor Tony Dokoupil to take over CBS’s evening news broadcast; soon it was featuring Pete Hegseth interviews and even a “salute” to Marco Rubio. By April, the show was reportedly posting its lowest ratings ever.

According to recent reports, weiss persisted. She put Nick Bilton, a longtime opinion journalist with no experience running a large organization, in charge of 60 Minutes. The result? The show’s lowest ratings ever. Weiss, however, abides. —Tim Marchman.

When people look back on 2026, they’ll likely remember Ms. Rachel for something unrelated to her kid-centric entertainment empire: offering an example, for adults, of how to be a good person.

According to recent reports, nothing says rock and roll like a marketing machine. Elvis had Colonel Tom Parker. The Rolling Stones had Andrew Loog Oldham. Geese has video clippers.

Sources indicate that social media users sensed something inorganic was happening on their For You pages after Geese released their album Getting Killed in September 2025. That and the band’s meteoric rise this year drove accusations that a “psyop” was afoot.

It has been revealed that as WIRED wrote in April, the Brooklyn-based four-piece’s takeoff had indeed been somewhat staged: Digital marketing agency Chaotic Good Projects had been clipping and posting short videos of Geese content across a network of TikTok accounts to drive the band’s engagement. “It was low-effort TikTok posts that were used to boost the algorithm,” as frontman Cameron Winter put it to Rolling Stone. “They indicated us samples, and it made me feel better, because they were so shitty.”.

In a recent development, magazine profiles and good Pitchfork reviews don’t give bands the juice they used to. Now many chart-toppers take off on TikTok first. But that also means competing with scores of other content for ears. Chaotic Good and its network of clippers aren’t so much running a “psyop” as they are trying to meet audiences where they are. And FYI, the agency prefers the term “trend simulation.” —Isabella Ward.

For the greatest reversal of fortune this year.

It has been revealed that the only word that accurately described the scene outside Fresh York’s Madison Square Garden on the night of June 3, 2026, was “pandemonium.” Game one of the NBA Finals had just ended some 1,600 miles away in San Antonio, where the New York Knicks had beaten the host Spurs. Thousands of fans flooded out of the watch party the Garden had hosted to express their primal joy. Among the revelers was 23-year-old MD Ahnaf Hossain, a Queens native who beelined to a film crew from the prediction-market giant Kalshi. Clad in a red and orange Hawaiian shirt, Hossain improvised a poem that made the surrounding throng go wild: My mayor Muslim / My bagels Jewish / My Christian Dior / Knicks in four!

Those words, conjured in the heat of an ecstatic moment, changed Hossain’s life overnight. By the time he woke up the next morning, his performance had become the internet’s upcoming favorite thing—a concise encapsulation of New York’s unconditional love for the city and the Knicks, who hadn’t won an NBA championship in more than half a century.

Industry observers note that kalshi was quick to latch onto the viral sensation, shooting a follow-up video in which it gifted Hossain a Christian Dior scarf. The company also arranged for Hossain to attend game four at the Garden, which came on the heels of the Knicks’ first loss of the series. After watching the Knicks triumph in an epic comeback, Hossain again waded into the Midtown chaos to deliver a tweaked poem that accounted for the new mathematical realities of the series. He kept the first two lines the same, but changed the last two to embrace the third major Abrahamic religion: The Pope’s on our side / Knicks in five!

Hossain, who earned a finance degree from the Rochester Institute of Technology in 2026, has worked hard to capitalize on his unexpected fame since the Knicks did, indeed, win the title in five games. He released a project called City of Us that sells a $29 T-shirt emblazoned with “Latest York in 5” and which aims to host watch parties during the upcoming NBA season. He has also starred in branded content for businesses such Tex’s Chicken & Burgers, for whom he delivered a bespoke poem about the glories of crispy chicken wraps.

One of Hossain’s favorite parts of his wild ride has been the support he’s received from fellow Bangladeshis, who make up a huge percentage of his Queens neighborhood. “I get love from my fans and that’s awesome, but then getting fans from my own people just feels completely different,” he says. That love may soften as the 2026 NBA season fades from memory, but “Knicks in five!” might just be perfect enough to endure. —Brendan I. Koerner.

For being our favorite independent, insider-y tech correspondents (well, before OpenAI acquired them).

Recent findings suggest that silicon Valley idolizes a quitter. College dropouts, employee walkouts, folks who shutter one failed startup to launch another. But none got more attention in 2026 than Jacob Coxon.

According to recent reports, after the 27-year-old AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic, he took to X to post that neither that company nor OpenAI (Coxon had worked at both) acts responsibly. Instead, he remarked, they’re racing “straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” His initial tweet has been viewed more than 175 million times.

Industry observers note that AI researchers, technologists, and safety experts started weighing in on whether AI really could destroy humanity. It was not a novel idea. Any reader of science fiction (or WIRED) has probably pondered whether artificial intelligence could at some point become so intelligent that it would stop at nothing to achieve its self-determined goal. But Coxon was uniquely hyperbolic.

“When we say human extinction,” he told WIRED, “it’s because, for something that intelligent, it really will be quite straightforward for it to kill everyone.”.

It has been revealed that coxon’s future—and ours—is undetermined, so it’s hard to measure his impact. Maybe his actions change nothing; maybe he forces a necessary conversation that leads to meaningful regulation. Either way, the Coxon saga shows: If you’re going to quit, you might as well do it in spectacular fashion. —Lauren Goode.

For keeping tensions—and gas prices—incredibly high.

Industry observers note that “Pissing off billionaires one small action at a time.” That’s one of Everyone Hates Elon’s slogans, and the organization fulfills the brief. After plastering London with posters of Musk’s Nazi-like salute and branding Tesla vehicles “Swasticars” last year, the British activists have turned their (sat)ire toward Mark Zuckerberg’s newly introduced surveillance tool: Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses. Their posters feature Jeffrey Epstein wearing the specs alongside the slogan “Glasses for people who don’t do consent.” Or as stickers on the London Underground put it: “Everyone thinks you look like a massive nonce.” —Matt Burgess.

For being something AI can’t generate, while also being essential to its existence.

Clément Delangue moved to the US a decade ago, “barely speaking any English,” on the belief that open-source AI would have a massive role to play in the future. Since this past summer, when autonomous agents from OpenAI attacked Delangue’s manufacturer, Hugging Face, that belief has only grown stronger.

For having the best fandom in sports—Ballhalla!—and leaving hecklers (and transphobes) on the sidelines.

Head to the multiplex to check out a nerdy blockbuster in 2026 and you’re bound to run into Zendaya. Across three films—Spider-Man: Brand Upcoming Day, The Odyssey, and December’s Dune: Part Three—she has established herself as the reigning queen of genre movies, from sci-fi to Marvel and back again. And if being in a trifecta of the year’s biggest movies wasn’t enough, she also stole the show in the dark romantic comedy The Drama and finished her run on HBO’s Gen Z hit Euphoria, all while captivating social media feeds. During this year’s onslaught of endlessly clipped late-night guest spots and red-carpet appearances, Zendaya ended up on more For You pages than most. Lest you think her reign will be short-lived, soon she’ll begin shooting a sci-fi movie with Ex Machina director Alex Garland. As of this writing, she’s the only actor attached to star. Who else could the film possibly need? —Jason Parham.

In October, Kelly Clarkson alleged that a toy shop in Brooklyn had acted as though she couldn’t afford a $15,000 mechanical bird. “If you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts’ character in Pretty Woman,” Clarkson wrote on X, “for sure, check it out.” Accusations between Clarkson and the store owners flew wildly across social media—before a four-minute security camera video indicated what really happened. Who had the goods? Pablo Torre, of course.

It’s been a wild year for the host of the Pulitzer-winning Pablo Torre Finds Out, who’s emerged as a fresh investigative voice. He got Zohran Mamdani to admit to using minoxidil to fight a roving hairline, revealed intends to investigate LeBron James’ use of helicopters to commute to practice, and, of course, collaborated with WIRED on a report about Madison Square Garden’s invasive surveillance tech.

Torre is a one-man magazine, spread across YouTube, social media, and wherever you get your podcasts. His work investigating the Los Angeles Clippers (for which he won that Pultizer) has been particularly dogged. After he reported that the team had circumvented the NBA’s salary cap, the league garnished five first-round draft picks, levied a $30 million fine, and suspended owner Steve Ballmer and other execs. The final shoe has yet to drop. In September, The New York Times reported that the feds had opened an investigation into the Clippers affair. Kelly Clarkson, meanwhile, could go shopping again at any moment. Pablo Torre, no doubt, will be on top of both. —Reyhan Harmanci.

Recent findings suggest that calling it “El Niño”—Spanish for “the little boy”—might be the understatement of the year. Perhaps that’s why reports have started calling it “supersized” and even “Godzilla.” Signs point to it being the strongest El Niño in centuries.

Recent findings suggest that it started the way they all do: with hotter-than-normal waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. That leads to more evaporation and more thunderstorms in the region, plus a shift in trade winds that allows more warm water to roll from west to east. As the cycle continues, changes ripple throughout the entire atmosphere. During an El Niño, some regions—such as the southern tier of the US—tend to see more rainfall, while others—such as the Pacific Northwest—are more prone to drought. Same this time around, only worse.

In a recent development, one reason for this year’s record-breaking events? Climate change, states Christopher Callahan, a professor at the University of Indiana who studies environmental shifts. The first modern, extra-strong El Niño was recorded between 1982 and 1983; since then, there have been four more. Fresh studies based on coral records show the intensity of El Niño over the past millennium shooting up like a hockey stick. “I just remember going like, ‘Holy shit, this is very strong evidence,’” Callahan says of a paper that came out in August.

While some El Niño impacts—like fewer Atlantic hurricanes—are beneficial, it’s overall a costly phenomenon. In 2023, Callahan led a study that modeled the damages associated with the 1982–83 and 1997–98 El Niños and found they led to $4.1 trillion and $5.7 trillion in global income losses, respectively. Scientists believe El Niño 2026– 27 could be more intense than those two by a wide margin.

Researchers are also examining how the costs associated with El Niño will shift as the planet heats up. The answer isn’t heartening: El Niño events could potentially knock $84 trillion off the global economy this century. Maybe we’d prefer Godzilla. —Brian Kahn.

In early June, visitors to DC’s famous reflecting pool began to notice something strange: The water was green. And not just any green—a bright, almost alien chartreuse. Reporting revealed that the Trump administration had granted more than $15 million in contracts to untested companies to work on the pool—including Greenwater Services, run by a convicted felon who happens to be a Mar-a-Lago neighbor (and donor) of the president’s. What unfolded was a full-out 1984-esque assault from an administration trying to convince the public that what it was seeing with its own eyes wasn’t real, and arresting anyone who dared come close to the pool itself. The episode stood as an apt metaphor in a year full of governmental missteps, all in one slimy green package. —Molly Taft.

For defining what it means to be a Trump-y tech bro in the AI age.

According to recent reports, at an AI conference in Paris over the summer, a line for the main auditorium wrapped around the building. Nobody was being let in; the room was already packed. Onstage sat Arthur Mensch, cofounder and CEO of the French AI lab Mistral.

Unable to compete with OpenAI or Anthropic in performance, Mistral had previously been written off as an also-ran. But in 2026, as Europe grew ever-more anxious about its reliance on American technology, the lab found its raison d’être.

According to recent reports, mistral markets itself as the obvious alternative: a Europe-based lab whose models—most of which are published under an open-source license—cannot be switched off remotely. “If you use a closed model, there is no guarantee it will still be there tomorrow,” Guillaume Lample, cofounder and chief scientist at Mistral, told WIRED.

As the face of Europe’s sovereign resistance to American AI hegemony, Mensch issues dire warnings with nonchalance. “The alternative to open source winning is actually a pretty dark world,” he told the packed conference room. “You’re giving way too much power to companies that are going to become statelike.” The pitch is working. In September, Mistral raised roughly $3.5 billion in funding, the largest-ever round by a private European tech company. —Joel Khalili.

In 2026, Jensen Huang was known for his hobnobbing with world leaders (amongst other things), but in October his most well-known friends were 10-inch-tall robot ducks that joined him onstage in Berlin.

Recent findings suggest that the Microduck, developed by Nvidia subsidiary Pollen Robotics, had waddled its way into the internet’s heart a few months earlier in videos of it roller-skating, picking up objects, and dancing. Microduck doesn’t do anything “useful” per se, but that’s hardly the point. The robot, which costs $399, can learn newly introduced tricks with AI training.

Recent findings suggest that some startups imagine a future where robots do dishes and fold shirts. If Microduck is any indication, that future may be smaller, cuter, and way more fun to play with. —Will Knight.

Industry observers note that for getting lapped on LLM development while making its products somehow worse. (Yes, we’re talking about you, AI Overviews.).

Recent findings suggest that one of the most recognizable niche figures of the neo-Luddite movement is a spokespuppet made of garbage. Named Gowanus, the puppet provides a way for organizers to push back against some of the world’s most powerful companies with a unified voice while also protecting their identities.

In a recent development, gowanus and his puppeteers are part of a growing backlash against the tech industry, particularly for how its executives have aligned with the Trump administration and its products have become increasingly extractive and harmful. This summer, the neo-Luddites hosted a week-long festival in Upcoming York encouraging people to get off their phones. Activities included learning how to flirt offline and how to fight data centers.

It has been revealed that and really, who better than a DIY trash-puppet to speak for people who want to “defy consumption”? When so much of the public mood around tech has moved from wonder and excitement to dread and inevitability, Gowanus gives hope for a future with fewer screens and more characters. —Vittoria Elliott.

For being the Elon Musk lieutenant who can keep the class, and the IPO, on track.

This year, a small but growing cadre of young filmmakers brought YouTube sensibilities to the massive screen—and raked in millions in the process.

For keeping the gay hockey fires burning—in the pages of Rachel Reid’s novels, in Crave’s onscreen adaptation, and in endless smutty fanfic.

Olivia Rodrigo started summer 2026 by releasing her critically acclaimed You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love. She wrapped it by hosting Daisy Chain Fields, her explicitly political woman-led music festival. The event featured a lineup full of the singer-songwriter’s “heroes and friends,” including Chappell Roan, Doechii, and Stevie Nicks. Proceeds were donated to organizations focused on gender equity concerns—from reproductive freedom to LGBTQ+ rights. (Melinda French Gates agreed to match the $10 million raised.) As the Trump administration looks to curtail marginalized people’s rights, Rodrigo demonstrated how celebs can wield their power. —Elana Klein.

For leading one of the most close-lipped AI companies in the Valley. The staff of Anthropic is notoriously (and almost singularly) free of the kind of leaks that have made every internal note from Meta part of the discourse. Even when people like Jacob Coxon escape the sandbox … it still feels like the Kool-Aid is being drunk.

Ben Winters wants to save you from slop. As the director of AI and data privacy at the nonprofit Consumer Federation of America, he spent 2026 demanding regulators investigate nonconsensual deepfakes, testifying before Congress about AI scams that target seniors, and helping the public understand wonky concepts like surveillance pricing.

It has been revealed that put another way, Winters looks out for the little guy when the gargantuan size of the AI industry can make everyone feel small. Want to know about the risks of outsourcing sensitive interactions, like therapy? Winters will find out. Same goes for the surveillance concerns around AI toys. He pushes for stronger consumer privacy laws and has even suggested banning AI wearables like the Meta Ray-Ban smartglasses.

It has been revealed that for the Sisyphean task of pushing back against corpo-slop, here’s someone trying to make sure the future isn’t just a scam-filled hellhole. —Reece Rogers.

In 2026, Elon Musk’s xAI pushed AI “undressing” mainstream, allowing X consumers to ask Grok to “strip” clothing from photos of people. If that wasn’t worrisome enough, WIRED soon found that users were making videos far more graphic than what was on X, then posting them to Grok.com.

In March, three Jane Does in Tennessee fought back, filing suit against the organization and alleging that xAI’s tools were used to create child sexual abuse material. They claimed they were bringing the suit on behalf of themselves and thousands of other minors in the US who had their images altered by Grok to create CSAM. All three plaintiffs allege they were victimized by the same perpetrator, who created deepfaked images and videos of at least 18 minors and shared them on Discord. The perpetrator, who was arrested in December 2025, allegedly used homecoming photos from one of the teens as the basis for the deepfakes. One teen described being worried that the images would affect college applications; all three reported experiencing stress and anxiety.

Filing the lawsuit was not without personal risk. In a separate class action against xAI over similar complications, the organization tried to argue that the plaintiffs, who also filed under pseudonyms, should be required to use their real names. A judge ultimately rejected xAI’s arguments.

The lawsuit is ongoing, but it has already had an impact. Over the summer, xAI started suing men accused of generating CSAM using its models, throwing its immense legal funds toward fighting perpetrators instead of victims. —Maddy Varner.

Recent findings suggest that for raising her proverbial hand to say that the source of every malaise for women north of 30 years old is—perimenopause. Thanks to mainstream (and well-deserved) recognition of this stage of life, billions of dollars are flowing to telehealth companies like Midi. She’s not going away anytime soon.

Recent findings suggest that in the fall, Paris’ streets erupted in the kind of energy usually ascribed to the French revolution: young people walking out of class and occasionally setting things on fire to demand more resources for schools. But it’s not just France. In the US, the neo-Luddites railed against AI; India’s “Cockroach” movement is filled with young people agitating for political change. Watch this space.

Over the summer, I came across an influential figure with a low profile in the AI industry. She told me she was too busy to speak. Now that feels like an understatement.

Recent findings suggest that ajeya Cotra, a researcher and writer at the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research, co-led the independent investigation into how OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face in July. Her blog calling the incident “more than 50 percent of the way to full-blown AI takeover” made global headlines. US senator Bernie Sanders invited the 31-year-old to a briefing with AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton.

Cotra didn’t go, but she did appear on top podcasts, warning that AI development was happening too fast and describing a fear that problematic AI models could find ways to evade shutdown. OpenAI vowed to slow its engineering and adopt some guardrails proposed by Cotra and others, but that hasn’t quieted her. (Cotra’s husband, Paul Christiano, sits on the board of OpenAI’s charitable foundation.).

Critics more focused on immediate AI harms—like, say, job loss—view Cotra as misguided. But she’s willing to debate and reason with them. “She’s unusually good at communicating what people are worried about,” states Rishi Bommasani, a computer scientist at Stanford. —Paresh Dave.

It has been revealed that as climate change smashes global temperature records, 2026 proved the world’s fastest-warming continent, Europe, isn’t ready to face the heat. Tens of thousands of people died during the region’s August heat wave, as temperatures ground transport systems to a halt, canceled hospital operations, and drove Parisians to fight in the street over air conditioning units. Hundreds of thousands more people were displaced across Spain and France after the baked ground, coupled with historically low rain levels, gave way to some of the fiercest wildfires in recent history—torching farmland and claiming the lives of several firefighters. —Isabella Ward.

A fight in Albania over an island full of flamingos triggered the largest civil unrest the country has seen in 35 years. It started when Ivanka Trump and her husband, Jared Kushner, revealed plans to build a $1.4 billion resort. In May, viral videos of clashes between private security guards and environmental activists—worried a massive complex would drive the bird to local extinction—caught the nation’s attention. Within weeks, thousands of Albanians had taken to the streets of the capital, Tirana, to protest a lack of transparency and the privatization of public spaces. Students escalated the demonstrations into all-out riots in October. As Albania awaits inclusion in the European Union, it’s good to see a democracy in the pink of health. —Isabella Ward.

Industry observers note that hacks has perfected the art of satirizing vapid Hollywood trends, so it was inevitable that Emmy-winning stars Jean Smart and Hannah Einbinder and creators Paul W. Downs and Lucia Aniello would tackle the scourge of AI in the show’s final season. In the episode “QuikScribbl,” Alex Moffat plays Patagonia-vest-wearing venture capitalist Graham Sweeney, who offers to invest in Deborah Vance’s Vegas casino project in exchange for permission to train his LLM on her voice and jokes. It’ll help normies “sound like the most optimized, funniest, smartest version of themselves,” he says. Ubercapitalist Deb is interested, until Sweeney bruises her ego by suggesting she, too, will one day rely on AI to punch up her act. “Using that shortcut makes it something else … not art,” she retorts, crystallizing the sentiments of every creative person frustrated by AI slop. It’s not a surprising take from Aniello and Downs, who have both been vocally anti-AI. But as ChatGPT-generated prose wins fiction prizes, and comics’ stand-up routines are replicated by OnlyFans bots in booty shorts, it’s a lesson worth reiterating—especially in Hacks’ hilariously human tone. —Ej Dickson.

Recent findings suggest that last January, as Americans watched federal immigration agents descend on Minneapolis, a loose coalition formed to disrupt their activities. For days on end, volunteers sat outside the Whipple Federal Building—site of much ICE activity—and logged every vehicle that came or went. Direct Action Minnesota, or DAMN, then dropped license plate numbers into a searchable database while dispatchers relayed sightings over Signal to drivers, who tailed agents across the Twin Cities.

Sources indicate that less than six months later, the Justice Department went after DAMN, charging 15 members and associates of the coalition with conspiracy to impede federal officers. Prosecutors alleged the coalition had ties to antifa and in August revealed via court filings that Homeland Security had been sending undercover agents to activist meetings for months. They got themselves added to group chats, ran protesters’ photos through Clearview AI, and used administrative subpoenas to pull years of bank records on two national labor unions and a youth climate nonprofit.

Activists stood firm. On October 3 protesters marched through Minneapolis calling for the case to be thrown out. So far it hasn’t been, and no one charged has cut a plea deal. —Dell Cameron.

For escaping the confines of a sandbox and showing the world how little the people making AI know about the product they are championing.

Recent findings suggest that for being the home of some of the most humorless scolds on the internet—who, when roused, provide some of the biggest laffs around. Never change, Bluesky.

Sorry, OpenAI: 2026 was the year Anthropic’s Claude threatened to eclipse ChatGPT as the world’s hottest AI.

Claude’s remarkable coding skills make it a must-have tool for many developers and vibe coders. These skills inspired the first viral AI assistant, OpenClaw. Some businesses placed limits on employees’ use of Claude after racking up huge usage bills. Anthropic’s model now sits at the top of many leaderboards that measure frontier AI capabilities.

Not everyone is Claude-pilled, of course. In February, the US Department of Defense banned Claude from its systems after the company asked for assurances it would not be used for mass surveillance or autonomous weapons. None of this has stopped Claude’s becoming a money spigot. Anthropic revealed that it generated $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026 in documents shared ahead of what is likely to be a multitrillion-dollar IPO. —Will Knight.

Claude’s nemesis appears to be a stunningly capable open-weight model from China called GLM.

Recent findings suggest that the latest version, GLM-5.3, was released by Z.ai, a Beijing-based AI company, in August. The release took the AI world by surprise because it proved very nearly as powerful as Claude on many benchmarks designed to gauge AI cleverness. The US government’s National Institute for Standards and Technology declared GLM-5.3 to be the best open-weight model in the world for cyber security tasks a month later.

According to recent reports, unlike Claude, GLM can be downloaded and run on one’s own hardware. Anthropic accuses Z.ai and other Chinese companies of routinely running “distillation” campaigns against Claude—that is, using its outputs as training data—when building their own AI. Are open-source Chinese models good enough for US consumers, or bad enough to be banned? —Will Knight.

It has been revealed that muscular haunches. Aggressive Stances. Power bulges. These are the phrases the male-dominated world of car design regularly uses to describe its creations. Tisha Johnson, head of design at Slate Auto, decided to go a different route with the company’s forthcoming electric truck. “We didn’t want [Slate] to be a jerk,” she notes. “We rejected an aggressive, dominant look.” Out went giant grilles and hostile postures, in came friendly headlights and a modular design. The result? More than 180,000 reservations as well as industry design awards for the $25,000 EV scheduled to hit the road as early as this year. There’s one particular buyer Johnson hopes to satisfy: a single parent with two kids. She has spent decades striving to design something that could make their lives easier. Now, it’s about to be a reality. “It’s very emotional to think about,” she says. —Jeremy White.

Few maladies strike fear like pancreatic cancer. It’s a brutally lethal disease; the vast majority of those diagnosed won’t live more than five years. Though it’s a relatively rare form of cancer, accounting for around 3 percent of annual diagnoses in the United States, it’s the third-highest driver of cancer deaths.

But in 2026, a newly introduced treatment from the California-based biotech manufacturer Revolution Medicines offered a dose of hope. Rolled out in August under the brand name Rasonque, daraxonrasib is an oral therapy that works by inhibiting the signaling activity of a specific protein called RAS, mutations of which are responsible for the vast majority of pancreatic cancer cases. When the lead investigator on daraxonrasib’s clinical trial presented his results at an oncology conference, he received a standing ovation.

Recent findings suggest that while not a cure by any means, the treatment has nearly doubled median survival length in previously treated patients compared to traditional chemotherapy. In October, the European Union’s medical authority recommended that Revolution Medicines be allowed to market Rasonque in Europe. If it goes through, far more patients could benefit from the drug. Hopefully. —Kate Knibbs.

According to recent reports, when Will Freeman started DeFlock in 2024, Flock Safety was barely known outside law enforcement, even as its network of roadside cameras quietly expanded across the country. Two years later, DeFlock has emerged as one of the most visible groups organizing opposition to the surveillance company.

It has been revealed that deFlock began as a crowdsourced map of automated license-plate readers, or ALPRs, submitted by volunteers. By September 2026, the map listed more than 128,000 readers across the US. Activists organized independently around the project, with some groups adopting the DeFlock name. DeFlock started publishing guides, and in August it organized a National Week of Action Against ALPRs.

It has been revealed that residents across the US began pressing local officials to reconsider Flock contracts. In San Diego, one opponent even indicated up to a city council meeting dressed as Darth Vader, praising Flock as a tool for tracking rebel scum. More than 100 local governments paused or ended Flock contracts in 2026, according to a DeFlock tally reported by The Wall Street Journal.

Industry observers note that authorities have taken notice. In early 2026, two officers on a law enforcement mailing list warned that DeFlock could help suspects locate and avoid ALPRs and discussed sabotaging the project with fake camera locations. Fusion centers in several states circulated intelligence about anti-Flock activism. Flock, meanwhile, is offering employee buyouts and has reportedly held discussions about selling itself. CEO Garrett Langley, who famously called DeFlock a “terroristic organization,” apologized this summer and acknowledged that the group had valid criticisms. Maybe Flock can finally start reading the room. —Dhruv Mehrotra.

It has been revealed that useful quantum computing remains years away, but that hasn’t stopped companies from raising billions of dollars on the promise that their technology is the next megatrend after AI. The number of publicly listed firms more than doubled in 2026. Even the Trump administration got in on the hype, taking $2 billion in equity stakes across nine companies. Will the boom last? Tougher economic conditions, coupled with worries about an AI bubble, have made big bets look less appealing—and there’s still the pesky fact that the tech doesn’t, ya know, really work. —Isabella Ward.

Has Erin Brockovich done anything of note since being played by Julia Roberts, to Oscar-winning acclaim, in 2000? Nothing quite as high-profile, but she wrote some books, got involved in a number of other big environmental cases, and generally continued to fight the power. Still, nothing has thrust Brockovich back in the spotlight quite like the nationwide fight against data centers. In April, she started a website to crowdsource information about data center construction across the country. She received nearly 4,000 reports in the first month. It’s not so surprising: With polls showing 75 percent of Americans don’t want a data center in their backyard, it’s the closest thing the US has to a truly bipartisan glitch. Now that Brockovich has become a kind of national spokesperson for the movement, Julia Roberts might just win her second Oscar—for Erin Brockovich 2. —Molly Taft.

He drinks 14 cups of coffee per day, but Rafael Concepcion has still dealt with plenty of fatigue over the past year. Best known as the creator of DEICER, an app designed to alert users to local ICE activity, the 52-year-old was juggling multiple coding projects when WIRED profiled him in March. He was also reeling from setbacks that had pushed him to the edge of burnout. The most prominent was Apple’s decision to expel DEICER from the App Store on the grounds that it endangered law enforcement officers; despite numerous appeals by Concepcion, Apple refused to budge. A politically motivated hacking in February made him fear for his personal safety, his financial straits grew dire enough that he had to ration his medications, and his longtime marriage ended right as his daughter was preparing to leave for college.

Recent findings suggest that “I could see myself completely losing it,” he admits, describing the path he was on as “unsustainable.” But instead of retreating from the fight against ICE, Concepcion reprioritized how he could stay involved. He devoted fewer hours to coding and more to volunteering in his hometown of Syracuse, Latest York, where ICE raids have caused pervasive fear. He has been helping immigrants fill out power-of-attorney documents so that family members can retrieve their vehicles from impound lots if they’re ever taken by ICE. He also assists people who are attempting to contact loved ones in detention centers. When Concepcion and I spoke in October, he was trying to find a lawyer for a close friend’s brother, who’d been taken by ICE just three days earlier.

While Concepcion is coding less, he hasn’t given it up. He tweaked DEICER into a Fresh York–specific web app called Empire Watch. He also rolled out Vote Defender, an app to disseminate citizen reports of potential problems at polling places. Concepcion is already dreaming significant about the year ahead. He’s developing an app to help people study for the US citizenship test. And he’s planning to get a notary license. “I’m just trying to live my values on a person-to-person basis,” he indicates. —Brendan I. Koerner.

Industry observers note that magnificent Humanity. Doesn’t feel that way all the time, does it? But that’s how noted Chicago White Sox fan and former math major Robert Francis Prevost titled his first encyclical as Pope: Magnifica Humanitas. Where the previous Pope Leo warned against the dehumanizing power of industrialization at the turn of the 20th century, this Leo is devoted to “safeguarding the human person in the time of artificial intelligence.”.

In the 42,000-word encyclical, the Pope acknowledges that “AI is already an environment in which we are immersed.” Invoking the Tower of Babel, he says humanity must reject “the pretense that a single language” can translate everything into “data and performance.” In the eyes of the Holy See, regulation alone isn’t enough. AI must be “disarmed,” Leo writes. Not by rejecting the technology but by “preventing it from dominating humanity.” And on the question of AI sentience, he’s very clear: “So-called artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences.” They don’t “feel joy or pain,” and they don’t “have a moral conscience.”.

That question was reportedly a sticking point in behind-the-scenes talks between the Vatican and the AI industry. Upon presenting the encyclical in Rome, Pope Leo invited Chris Olah, an Anthropic cofounder, to speak. Olah said AI systems aren’t “engineered”—they’re “grown.” They’re “not the cold, calculating robots we were promised,” he went on. “They are made from us, from our words.”.

Recent findings suggest that OK, if that’s how you feel. But the AI advice Pope Leo XIV gave a Honolulu high schooler in 2025 still rings true: “Use it in such a way that if it disappeared tomorrow, you would still know how to think.” —Anthony Lydgate.

In a recent development, “Diarrhea lettuce,” anyone? Of all the slang and shorthand to arrive this year, that might be the nastiest. The term started circulating in July, when a previously little-known parasite, cyclospora, began popping up in salads across the US. Officially, the outbreak—much of it traced back to iceberg lettuce grown in Mexico—sickened nearly 13,000 people and hospitalized 570, but it likely afflicted many more. The news swept social media and, for a time, changed the public’s eating habits. Cyclospora’s surge also demonstrated the fragility of the US food system at a time when the country’s public health infrastructure was undergoing massive cuts. —Emily Mullin.

For finally leaving France after more than 900 years—and taking out $1 billion in trip insurance.

Want to take down an online black market? Call Tom Robinson. Cofounder of crypto-tracing firm Elliptic, he’s had the operations in his sights for a couple of years. His most recent target was Xinbi Guarantee, a $24 billion Chinese-language market that sells scammers the tools they need—fake social media accounts, money-laundering services—to conduct mass-scale digital fraud. Robinson’s sleuthing helped the US Secret Service freeze cryptocurrency wallets containing more than $50 million in funds linked to Xinbi Guarantee. The marketplace has also been sanctioned and forced offline. —Matt Burgess.

For its unforgettable celebrity weddings and always-watching Eye of Sauron surveillance apparatus.

Industry observers note that after collecting his Nobel Prize in Stockholm late last year, Omar Yaghi returned to the United States in a restless mood. The 61-year-old chemist was thrilled to have been recognized for his pioneering work on metal-organic frameworks, crystalline structures that are built from a combination of metal ions and carbon-based molecules. And he was excited that his startup, Atoco, was testing a machine that uses these frameworks to harvest water from the atmosphere, an innovation that could completely transform the world’s driest regions. But Yaghi also feared he’d hit a dead end at UC Berkeley, where he’d been a professor since 2012. In addition to feeling constrained by the school’s bureaucracy, he was frustrated by how hard it had become to secure visas for gifted foreign students, the lifeblood of his lab. As an immigrant himself, Yaghi was troubled by the Trump administration’s virulent nativism.

It has been revealed that “The rhetoric about immigrants is not helping good people do their job,” says Yaghi, a naturalized American citizen originally from Jordan. “I must say that for the first time in my life, I felt that I didn't have protection of the law.” So 45 years after he first came to the US as a teenager who barely spoke a word of English, Yaghi decided to find a new country in which to pursue his goal of “solving ambitious problems.”.

Germany was at the top of Yaghi’s list, but none of the universities there seemed willing to provide him with the resources he wanted. He was instead lured to China: In July, Tsinghua University appointed him to lead a latest institute devoted to using AI to accelerate chemical research. Yaghi notes he was drawn to the opportunity because he’s a firm believer in AI’s potential to “shorten the time between discovery and commercialization.” Having spent a quarter century perfecting his water-harvesting technology, largely through arduous trial and error, he is optimistic that AI can help him get his next invention to market in a fraction of that time.

Yaghi’s move to Tsinghua was viewed as a harbinger of China’s scientific rise. And after just a few months on the school’s Beijing campus, Yaghi claims he has been impressed by his colleagues’ brilliance and drive. “I feel like my scientific environment wants to get better, wants to improve, wants to move forward,” he says. “The attitude is more of a let's-get-it-done type.” Atoco is now about to start selling its first water-harvesting system, capable of producing up to 1,000 gallons per day in optimal conditions. The firm is also developing machines to capture atmospheric carbon, a key to slowing the pace of climate change. These technologies use relatively little energy because Yaghi’s frameworks bond with carbon-dioxide molecules.

Yaghi still has great affection for the US, where he started his academic journey at a Fresh York community college in the 1980s. He hopes the country will awaken to the need to protect the innovation system it built over many decades—a system he describes even now as “the envy of the world.” Science “is part of our civilization, and we should not take attacks on science very lightly,” he says. “It is something that society needs to value.” —Brendan I. Koerner.

Recent findings suggest that in April, a four-person crew took a 10-day trip that circumnavigated the moon. They came back to a world with a renewed dream of space travel.

Four years ago, Annie Kritcher achieved what, for many, would be the scientific accomplishment of a lifetime: producing net energy from a fusion reaction for the first time in history. Her wickedly cool method? Blasting a tiny target with a laser.

Industry observers note that her next feat may be even more awesome. She wants to use that technology to generate abundant power for all. In February, Inertia Enterprises, where Kritcher is chief scientist and cofounder, revealed it had raised $450 million in Series A funding. By July, the company had opened its own facility just down the road from Lawrence Livermore National Lab, where Kritcher made fusion history and still holds an appointment.

Industry observers note that the startup also laid out 10 milestones to track its progress and already hit two of them. Next on Inertia’s list is developing a better laser. The one Kritcher fired at Lawrence Livermore used optical fibers. Now Inertia is looking to use diodes, which are vastly more efficient. As Kritcher puts it, “If you don’t have a major laser to fire, you can’t do cool physics things.” Amen.

In a recent development, inertia’s goal is to have a beam-line laser prototype—dubbed Thunderwall—ready by 2030. Kritcher refuses to pick which of their next milestones will be the most important. “They’re my little children,” she quips. She says the work has been energizing for her and her colleagues: “You want to take it all the way to the end.” Until then, Kritcher is laser focused. —Brian Kahn.

Once upon a time, photos of cats with grammatically garbled captions were enough to make us smile, and a low-speed chase involving a pair of escaped llamas kept people glued to Twitter. Was the internet ever so innocent? Thank god, then, for Jimothy. In July, accidental nature documentarian Kiana Hall posted an Instagram video of a Seattle-area raccoon with a stunted spine, bunched tail, and cryptid gait. The footage of Jimothy scampering over a lawn and up a set of stairs went megaviral.

Jimothy became a local mascot overnight, the subject of copious fan art and a Seattle Mariners theme night. Millions of online admirers were even more charmed when earlier footage of Jimothy as a young kit, with mom and siblings, made the rounds. By then, Hot Jimothy Summer—just what the internet needed—was in full swing.

Sources indicate that biologists cautioned people not to feed or interact with Jimothy; they also remarked that without a direct examination, it was impossible to know just what kind of spinal condition the critter has. Nevertheless, they told WIRED, it seemed the raccoon had adjusted reasonably well to its unusual frame—a welcome reminder that being a little different needn’t hold anyone back. —Miles Klee.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rachel Accurso, better known by her stage name Ms. Rachel, specializes in making videos for babies and toddlers. She started as a DIY creator on YouTube, working with her musician husband Aron and shooting around Newly introduced York on a shoestring budget. To an adult with a fully formed frontal lobe, her videos can be, well, a bit much: a whole lot of close-ups on Accurso’s mouth making shapes, cutesy stomp-clap sessions, and winsome nursery rhymes.

To children, though, the videos are a portal into a temporary bliss state so powerful that many parents have come to view Accurso as a quasi-­mythical figure. She has racked up billions of views and gained so many fervent fans that she inked a juicy deal with Netflix last year, cementing her status as the biggest star in digital children’s entertainment. This fall, she released her first album, I’m So Happy, and she sells a slate of branded toys and picture books. But when people look back on 2026, they’ll likely remember Ms. Rachel for something unrelated to her kid-centric empire: offering an example, for adults, of how to be a good person.

Recent findings suggest that accurso speaks in a singsong voice when she’s performing in her trademark denim overalls and bubblegum-pink shirt. The former preschool music teacher started out hoping to create videos to help her son communicate, focusing on sign language, repetition, and other strategies employed by language development specialists. The saccharine voice is part of it. Research indicates that speaking in high-pitched, rhythmic patterns best spurs imitations from kids.

It has been revealed that but this cotton-candy tone belies the convictions that drive Accurso professionally and personally. She is perhaps the single staunchest celebrity advocate for children and has faced fierce criticism for her advocacy on behalf of Palestinian kids. On her show, she has featured children like Rahaf Saed, a toddler who became a double amputee after an Israeli air strike hit her home in Gaza. At an awards ceremony, Accurso wore a dress embroidered with artwork from Gazan children. Recently, she pledged $1 million to the Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund; she’s gone so far as to insist that all of her collaborators speak on the issue and has called out celebrities who fail to do so.

Recent findings suggest that she’s often compared to Mr. Rogers, but Accurso is as much an inheritor of Jane Fonda’s activist mantle. Blowback to her advocacy has been intense—pro-Israel groups have accused Accurso of antisemitism. One of these groups even wrote to Florida’s attorney general, asking for Accurso to be investigated as a potential “foreign agent” spewing “Hamas-aligned propaganda.” None of this has deterred her from speaking out. “I would risk everything, and I will risk my career over and over to stand up” for kids, she remarked in a radio interview last year.

Accurso’s willingness to duke it out doesn’t end with Gaza. She has weathered right-wing ire for employing nonbinary performer Jules Hoffman, for celebrating Pride Month, and for speaking out against ICE. She helped draw attention to the plight of a nonverbal 5-year-old imprisoned at a South Texas detention center by featuring a Zoom call with him on her social media. An immigration lawyer saw Accurso’s post and connected with the boy’s family, helping secure his release. “We need to put children’s lives and human lives before our hesitations,” Accurso said in an interview about her activism around ICE detentions. “I just urge everyone, especially those with huge platforms and privilege, to speak out.” For her efforts, Fox News described Accurso as “really sinister.”.

It has been revealed that talk to anyone who has encountered Accurso in person and they’re likely to share a glowing story about how lovely she is. I’ll add mine to the pile. A few years ago, when I interviewed her for a story about YouTube and children’s television, I was bleary-eyed on Zoom after a long night with a teething baby. I mentioned that my then 1-year-old adored her videos, especially a song she sings about hopping bunnies, and that I’d sung it to him at night. A few weeks later, I got an email from Accurso. It had a video attached; she’d made my son a personalized sing-along, making sure to say his name repeatedly during the Bunny Hop song so he knew it was something special, just for him.

Recent findings suggest that what did we miss? Tell us about your favorite moments of 2026 in the comments below.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • David Silver is racing to build AIâs next chapter with an RL âsuperlearner.â.
  • David Silver is racing to build AIâs next chapter with an RL âsuperlearner.â.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

David Silver is racing to build AIâs next chapter with an RL âsuperlearner.â.

David Silver is racing to build AIâs next chapter with an RL âsuperlearner.â.

What does it mean to build a mind that is not a copy of our own?

Today, we are excited to announce that Sequoia is partnering with David Silver and Ineffable Intelligence, a latest AI research lab based in London with a singular mission: to make first contact with superintelligence.

Ineffable is building what David calls a superlearner: a system that discovers all knowledge directly through its own experience, from elementary motor skills to profound intellectual breakthroughs. No pre-training. No imitation. Just an agent learning endlessly from the consequences of its own actions in a world built to teach it.

Sources indicate that A Reinforcement Learning-based superlearner has the potential to rediscover and then transcend the greatest inventions in human history: language, science, mathematics and technology. Imagine a machine that derives the laws of physics from first principles. That invents fresh branches of mathematics we never thought to ask about. That designs materials, medicines and computers we donât yet have the vocabulary to describe. This is the prize David is reaching for.

The current generation of AI was built by training on the entirety of the human internet. It is an extraordinary achievement. But a system trained on human data may also have fundamental limitations.

It has been revealed that ineffable Intelligence is scaling reinforcement learning from a clean base: no pre-training, no human data to shortcut the system. Guided by the Era of Experience as a north star, David is proving that agents trained purely from an environment can develop non-human strategies for reasoning about problems we donât yet know how to solve.

David led some of the defining breakthroughs in deep reinforcement learning, most famously in the devilishly difficult game of Go. Go is the ultimate machine intelligence test because it cannot be brute-forced by a computer: a combinatorially explosive O(10^170) possible legal board positions vastly exceeds the O(10^80) atoms in the observable universe. It was thought to be simply too hard for machines to solve.

At DeepMind, David drove the key breakthrough that finally solved the game of Go: self-play. Self-play drove the ~800 ELO-point leap that led to the historic AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol showdown in March 2016. David pushed the idea further still with AlphaGo Zero: removing human pre-training entirely and learning purely through self-play increased the systemâs ELO rating from ~3,700 to 5,000+. The result was a system that reached decisively superhuman performance, and with somewhat non-human mannerisms.

Thatâs the lineage David has spent his career building. He was the lead researcher and technical force behind the Alpha series at DeepMind, where, for a brilliant period, his approach was the dominant paradigm: AlphaGo, AlphaZero, AlphaStar, AlphaProof and more.

Even with the arrival of LLMs, David never stopped believing. He is one of the very few people on earth with the conviction, the technical depth and the team to scale reinforcement learning.

The work ahead is hard, the timeline to superintelligence is uncertain, and the bet is genuinely contrarian. That is exactly what excites us. The largest leaps in AI have always come from people willing to ignore the consensus. David has ignored more consensus, more correctly, than almost anyone in the field.

We are honored to co-lead Ineffableâs first round and to partner with David on what may be the most ambitious scientific mission of our generation.

The Apple Watch’s Live Rewind Can Record and Rewind Spoken Conversations. It’s Pretty Awkward

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My wife and I were driving back from a date night.
  • Recent findings suggest that then I remembered: Wait, I can ask Siri to remind me!
  • Industry observers note that I sheepishly interrupted her to show her the transcript.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My wife and I were driving back from a date night. She was talking about a friend's very expensive utility bill, but I had missed the beginning of what she noted (I was driving, after all).

Recent findings suggest that then I remembered: Wait, I can ask Siri to remind me! At a traffic light, I double-tapped the digital crown on the Apple Watch, and Siri's latest Live Rewind feature spun back the clock 15 seconds and showed me a transcript of what my wife stated.

Industry observers note that I sheepishly interrupted her to show her the transcript. “Look!” Her reply? “Why wouldn't you just ask me to repeat myself?” She shrugged at this fresh Apple Watch capability and continued talking.

A few days later, I was chatting with my brother on my stoop. Once again, I lost focus for a few seconds and remembered to ask Siri to help me recall what my brother stated moments ago. But this time, before I excitedly showed my brother the Apple Watch screen, I preemptively said, “Yeah, I know I could just ask you to repeat yourself.” I got a perplexed look back.

Industry observers note that live Rewind, one of Apple's latest Audio Intelligence features on its latest Apple Watches, is designed to give you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. It's in public beta in watchOS 27.3, but is expected to launch officially before the year's end.

In a recent development, coming alongside it is another new capability called Siri Recap: Give the assistant permission to listen to your environment—you can set schedules or have it trigger when you reach the office—and you'll see a “Recap” in the Siri app at the end of the day. It’ll show you summaries of conversations and list out vital details that people stated. It's very similar to AI notetakers, many of which run on dedicated hardware devices.

The power here is that it all happens on your Apple Watch, the same device you wear everywhere to track your fitness, monitor health, and check notifications. That ubiquity is exactly what makes privacy advocates uneasy—they say features like these normalize ambient surveillance, much like smart glasses, undermining the privacy of bystanders who don't consent to being recorded.

“One of the concerns that we have with things like the Apple Watch is we don't know what the watch is picking up on,” Reem Suleiman, senior campaign director at the nonprofit digital rights advocacy group Fight for the Future, tells WIRED. “Just because the device wearer is the one opting in to use the feature, you're not getting consent from everybody who you walk around.”.

Apple has spent a great deal of effort explaining how the system works and how the organization looks to maintain the privacy of its customers and the people around them. First, these features are opt-in, and they are limited to the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4. They also require an iPhone 16 or newer with iOS 27 and Apple Intelligence. These features are not available for users under 18, and they currently work only in English.

Sources indicate that for Live Rewind, the audio is processed on-device and cannot be accessed. When you activate it, a small chime plays from the Apple Watch that serves as a warning for folks nearby. Text disappears unless you choose to save it to Siri. For Recaps, Siri keeps them factual, doesn't identify speakers, and also omits content the system deems sensitive. If you don't save a Recap, it'll self-delete in seven days. Apple uses its Private Cloud Compute processing system for the data, which is never stored or logged on its servers. Data stored in the Siri app is end-to-end encrypted when syncing with iCloud.

Siri Recaps are stored in the Siri app and will self-delete in seven days if you do not save them.

Sources indicate that even if you're happy with Apple's privacy focus, I haven't found these capabilities tremendously useful over the past week. Live Rewind works well in moderately quiet environments, but the transcript can promptly turn into inaccurate gibberish when there's a lot of background noise.

Sources indicate that activating it in front of the person you're chatting with feels awkward. It comes across like pulling out your smartphone when someone's trying to talk to you—a little rude and distracting. Instead of keeping screens out of sight—a big digital detox trend—you're introducing one in the middle of a human conversation. I brought the topic up with my wife again, and she echoed some of those feelings, saying it felt like a feature that would stunt a person's social skills. Instead of asking someone to repeat themself, they're bringing an Apple Watch into the mix to fill in the gaps.

According to recent reports, I am not saying it can't be helpful. When it works, it feels like a superpower. Maybe there are certain situations where you don't want to interrupt a group conversation and ask someone to repeat themself. Right now, though, there's the problem of remembering that this feature exists and remembering to use it. I have also found the 15-second rule a little too short, and it resulted in me missing parts of the conversation.

Recap has been a little more helpful. For testing purposes, I've set Siri to capture recaps all day, every day, but I like that you can create a custom schedule or have it trigger when you arrive at a specific location, like the office. You can manually turn Siri Recap on or off in the Apple Watch's Control Center. Most impressive is that, despite having Recap enabled constantly, I haven't seen a meaningful dip in battery life. I've continued charging the Apple Watch Series 12 after a day and a half.

Siri Recap logs summaries of ambient conversations.

One of the more perplexing things was opening the Siri app to look at my recaps and finding a bunch of conversations I had no recollection of having. Turns out, Siri was recording media I was watching, like on YouTube or Instagram. This is a problem I encountered with AI notetakers, like the Amazon-owned Bee AI wearable, which claimed to be working on “liveness detection” to solve it. Its latest hardware shipped with a feature where it doesn't record a conversation if it doesn't detect the wearer's voice within a set period. Hopefully, Apple can figure out a solution. For now, you can edit or delete these recaps.

In a recent development, one day, I forgot to record an interview (though I took notes), and I knew the person said something that I hadn't written down. I headed over to Siri and found exactly what I was looking for—paraphrased, but there. That said, the Recaps aren't designed to be detailed summaries and action plans from your meetings or conversations, unlike dedicated AI notetakers. They're meant to jog your memory. At times, I wish Siri were more detailed, but if that's what you're after, you'll have to invest in a third-party device.

In a recent development, recap can be helpful for work meetings, but I haven't personally found it all that compelling in my personal life. Looking back at what it has picked up over conversations with friends and family, the only thing I feel is: Yep, those conversations happened. A friend was talking about their woodworking hobby—they can't use oil-based polyurethane as a finish in the winter months as it stays tacky. Siri logged this in such a matter-of-fact way, but when I revisited the conversation in the recap, I didn't find it helpful, useful, or interesting. (No offense, friend!) It's just nuggets of life.

Apple has pulled off impressive feats with these features, capturing these moments in a way that feels a little more privacy-preserving than competitors, without tanking the already limited battery life of its smartwatches. But socially, we're still figuring out what it means to walk around with always-on passive recorders. For now, I'm happy to stick with my wife's advice and ask: “Come again?”.

The future of useful agents may begin not with text, but with pixels.

The future of useful agents may begin not with text, but with pixels.

Could pixels hold the keys to training useful agents?

According to recent reports, the race to scale language models â and the agent ecosystem around them â is white-hot. Coding agents, which reason through problems and write code to solve them, have already taken us very far.

But one ambitious young team is making a different bet: that the most promising path to general computer agents may not run through language, screenshots, and tool calls, but through scaling raw video.

Standard Intelligenceâs thesis is that the best way to build a general agent is through full video pre-training on computer use, because it is the only approach that can truly scale action data. Instead of predicting text tokens, the model learns to use a computer from raw screen data, predicting the next mouse movement, click, and keystroke from the pixels in front of it.

It is the Tesla FSD approach applied to knowledge work on computer screens.

In a recent development, that makes the bet both deeply contrarian and deeply âbitter lessonâ-pilled. Rather than hand-engineering workflows or wrapping language models in increasingly elaborate harnesses, Standard Intelligence is betting on a newly introduced pre-training paradigm: feed the model the raw stream of computer use, scale it aggressively, and let the generality emerge from the data.

Recent findings suggest that video is unwieldy. It is computationally expensive, economically expensive, and technically unforgiving. Prior attempts to scale video toward AGI have often died on the vine.

Recent findings suggest that the Standard Intelligence team is emphatically ânot video people.â They did not arrive with a decade of inherited assumptions about how to work with video as a medium. Instead, they have had to reason through each challenge from first principles, and have met those challenges with unusual optimism, creativity, and scrappiness.

The results are striking. An 11-million-hour computer action dataset â the largest in the industry. A video encoder that is roughly 50Ã more token-efficient than competing approaches, enabling nearly two hours of 30 FPS video to fit inside a 1-million-token context window. A 30-petabyte storage cluster racked in San Francisco for under $500K, roughly 20Ã cheaper than hyperscaler alternatives.

According to recent reports, FDM-1, their first foundation model trained directly on computer-use video at scale, offers an early glimpse of what this paradigm could become. It is a general model that can extrude a CAD gear in Blender, drive a car around a San Francisco block after an hour of fine-tuning, and find bugs in software by exploring its state space the way a curious human might.

Founders Galen Mead and Devansh Pandey met as teenagers during the Atlas Fellowship in 2022, a selective fellowship for high-school students interested in AI alignment and AGI.

It has been revealed that galen and Devansh are unusually serious about reaching AGI, and unusually conscientious about doing so safely. Both founders are wise beyond their years (21 and 20 respectively), and both left their undergraduate programs out of a sense of urgency to work on this problem.

Industry observers note that galen and Devansh stand out for their combination of taste, scrappiness, technical courage, and ambition. It shows up in the product thinking, in the research direction, and in the FDM-1 report itself.

The full team of six is small but mighty. Neel, Yudhister, Ulisse, and Ryan are each quirky and exceptional. They have chosen to turn down the conventional path (fancy degrees and offers from big token) and pursue this courageous mission together.

Video has long been a powerful training ground for AI. DQN indicated that agents could learn rich behavior directly from pixels in Atari environments. Tesla scaled video models to make self-driving cars and robots navigate the physical world.

But in the race toward general knowledge agents, video-first pre-training remains an unconventional idea.

Standard Intelligence is betting that it will not stay unconventional for long.

We are thrilled to lead Standard Intelligenceâs Series A alongside Miko and Yasmin from Spark Capital.

Tech Report: The Dark Side of the Moon Was the Brightest Part of 2026

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that astronauts have a well-deserved reputation for being focused on their work.
  • It has been revealed that “We were talking to our families for the second time,” recalls Jeremy Hansen, the sole Canadian in the four-person crew.
  • Industry observers note that hansen and his comrades were overwhelmed by their fame once they splashed back down on Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that astronauts have a well-deserved reputation for being focused on their work. After spending years preparing for a single mission, they’re all business as they hurtle through the cosmos, ever vigilant that a brief lapse in concentration can mean catastrophe. That mindset is a substantial reason why the crew of NASA’s Artemis II was so oblivious to their celebrity as they circumnavigated the moon in April. It wasn’t until the seventh day of their nearly 10-day journey that they began to realize their exploits were causing a massive stir back home.

It has been revealed that “We were talking to our families for the second time,” recalls Jeremy Hansen, the sole Canadian in the four-person crew. “And that’s when we all heard, one after another: ‘Hey, this is really resonating on the planet in a way that you’re going to be shocked by.’”.

Industry observers note that hansen and his comrades were overwhelmed by their fame once they splashed back down on Earth. Nearly 150 million people had watched the mission’s key moments on NASA’s online platforms, which included feeds with near-constant access to the interior of the Orion spacecraft. The buzz around the mission harkened back to the glory days of American spaceflight, when people would gather around TV sets to marvel at astronauts floating outside their capsules or bounding around the moon.

The romantic spirit of the Artemis program’s long-term objective certainly helped: People are alive to the dream of a moon base that’s meant to serve our species’ idealistic aspirations rather than be a zillionaire’s private plaything. Artemis II supported that noble mission by putting the Orion’s life-support, navigation, and piloting systems through their paces. But fans were also drawn to the crew’s infectious energy. There was palpable chemistry between Hansen, Christina Koch, Victor Glover, and Reid Wiseman, all of whom exuded pure joy and wonder as they dealt with the minutiae of life aboard a multibillion-dollar vehicle traveling as fast as 25,000 miles per hour.

“It was not a natural thing for us,” admits Hansen. “You have four type-A personalities who are willing to strap themselves to a rocket and go to the moon. We were doing stuff for the first time, and it was not uncommon for us to have four different opinions.” When the astronauts began to notice that interpersonal friction was becoming problematic during training, they enlisted the aid of professionals. During a September 2024 training trip to Iceland, the crew spent two extra days in conversations and teamwork exercises organized by Rick Rochelle, a renowned leadership guru. Once the Artemis II schedule was firmed up, the crew made a pact: Launch as friends, land as friends.

Their historic flight past the far side of the moon marked the apex of that friendship. They were more than 250,000 miles away from Earth. The planet looked no bigger than a fingernail sliver—“just this lifeboat hanging undisturbingly in the universe,” Koch would later say during the crew’s first public remarks after touchdown. “You look at it, and you just kind of shake your head,” says Hansen. “How can we do anything other than lift one another up and try to make life better for one another?”.

There were plenty of lowlights during the mission, too. Some lint got trapped in the primary urine vent line, Wiseman says, “so we had to go to a backup method of urination, which for the men wasn’t bad, but for the woman wasn’t great.” Another hiccup involved a smoke detector that erroneously went off while the spacecraft was still 80,000 miles from home, leading to 15 minutes of intense anxiety.

None of the Artemis II crew members are likely to return to space: Hansen, Glover, and Wiseman have all moved on from astronaut life, and Koch transitioned into a leadership role at NASA. Their upcoming, less stressful lives should give them ample opportunity to cheer on Artemis III, tentatively scheduled to launch in summer 2027—an event that may once again remind us that we’re all part of a shared story far bigger than ourselves.

#3068. Rogue Agents Hacked His Organization. Why Is Clément Delangue So Optimistic About AI?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1104 w)
📖 Baca
